subsubtopic: CLOSING OF HIGH TECHNOLOGY INDUSTRIES-IMPACT ON MONTREAL REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, things look pretty bleak in Montreal East. Thousands of jobs are in danger, now that Bombardier, Vickers, Gulf and other companies will have to close because three major industries in Montreal East have closed down.
The Prime Minister was supposed to create thousands of jobs as soon as he came to power. And now, a year later, they are closing down our hi-tech industries in Montreal East and thousands of jobs will be lost.
The Conservative Government has made no attempt to boost the morale of employees in the various industries who are about to lose their jobs. It had no hesitation, however, in handing over one billion dollars to Gulf and Petro-Canada, for a transaction that will take away 1,000 jobs from Montrealers.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious the Conservative leader has kept the habits he had when he was president of Iron Ore, because now he is Prime Minister of Canada, he wants to close down an industry in Montreal East.

Mr. Speaker, during Family Week it is important to consider what can be done to reduce the high incidence of family violence in Canada. One in 10 women, or about 750,000 women, will be beaten this year by their partners.
Battering another human being is a criminal offence. Doctors, police, and parliamentarians must not cover up or avoid dealing with domestic violence. Incidents must be dealt with openly, not condoned with silence. Police officers must be trained to deal with family violence and the laying of appropriate charges. Doctors must be able to recognize abuse in order to help women. Governments must provide shelter and financial assistance for battered families. Treatment groups for batterers and support groups for victims also need funding.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised that the Government would take initiatives to fund more tansition houses. Yesterday the Minister responsible for the Status of Women (Mr. McLean) said that this is a number one priority. However, discussions with the provinces are not enough. Again I ask that 3 per cent of the money used for the bank bail-out be used to fund 300 new transition houses.

Mr. Speaker, a recent article in The Toronto Star claims that, in the political world of Ottawa, science simply does not rate. Clearly, Mr. Speaker, this is not the case. Our Government is committed to encouraging scientists, universities and businesses to fulfil their research and development potential.

Canada is a rich country. Our population is well educated, our natural resources abundant and our industrial base is sound. If Canadians want to continue to succeed on the international market, they will have to raise the level and improve the effectiveness of their investments in research and development.

Canada's record of accomplishments in research and development is impressive, beginning with Mr. Bell's telephone in 1874 and ranging to the Canadarm of today. These achievements are a source of national pride. Encouraging further achievements poses an important challenge for the Government, for industry, and for the universities. Accordingly, the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Siddon) has identified three priority areas through which we can strenghten our ability to use our resources.
The first priority is encouraging innovation in the private sector. Second, we need a mechanism for monitoring the relevance and quality of research. The third and perhaps most important priority is education. As the Minister has said, we cannot do anything in science and technology without people. I say that we cannot hire and train the people without the necessary funding.

subsubtopic: HIJACKING OF ITALIAN CRUISE SHIP ACHILLE LAURO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Italian community of Canada was both shocked and concerned at the news two days ago that terrorist commandos hijacked the Italian cruise liner Achille Lauro, already referred to as the "ship of doom", thus threatening the lives of more than 400 people, innocent victims, the most of whom are of Italian origin.
The Government of Canada strongly condemns this act of terrorism, something that cannot be condoned no matter where it occurs or the cause it is supposed to serve.
Mr. Speaker, considering the very difficult situation now facing the Italian Government, I shall, if I may, as a representative of the Italian community in Canada, express the support of our Government and of the Canadian people for the Italian Government.
We earnestly hope that the hijack victims will be promptly released, through peaceful means and not by resorting to force.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of the House the deplorable condition of Prince Edward Island harbours. Wharves in Prince Edward Island that need immediate repair are being washed into the sea. The Government will not give an inch. It has turned a blind eye and a deaf ear toward fishermen.
To illustrate my point, on September 28 the fishermen at West Point Harbour spent the night at the wharf waiting for Hurricane Gloria to wash out their partially completed breakwater. Luckily Gloria was a spent force by the time it reached Prince Edward Island. If it had not been, the harbour and boats would have been destroyed. Even a sea turtle which swam into the harbour for protection left before morning to seek a safer haven.
In addition, a further section of wharf can no longer be used to tie up boats, another section is washing away, and pavement is sinking into the sea creating great holes in the wharf. Fishermen would have no worries if the planned wharf construction had beeen completed this year. If the Government does not act with celerity and fix the wharfs at Cape Egmont, West Point, Higgin's Wharf and many other places, the cost of repairs will increase as each day passes.
My repeated requests to the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans have not been acted upon. I fear that the plight of Island fishermen will go unnoticed even longer under the Acting Fisheries Minister (Mr. Nielsen). The Hon. Minister
has so many portfolios on his plate that I am sure these concerns will be shoved aside.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) so often boasts of acting with celerity on urgent matters. The state of small craft harbours in P.E.I. is an urgent and important matter. Can the Acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Nielsen) not see that? I urge him to act with celerity and fix these wharves immediately.

subsubtopic: USE OF VIOLENCE IN MIDDLE EAST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week Canadians were shocked and dismayed by the Israeli bombing of PLO Headquarters in Tunis. This week we have the same reaction to the PLM's hijacking of an Italian cruise ship. To the best of our knowledge no Canadians were on board the Achille Lauro when it was hijacked two days ago. However, all Canadians must join in condemning the growing cycle of terrorism and violence poisoning international relations in the Middle East.
Israel maintains that it will not give in to terrorists or bargain with black mail. We can understand that. But claiming to fight terror with terror is only another way of giving in to the terrorists-of letting them decide the rules of the game. Neither the Israelis nor the Palestinians can achieve their goals by the use of terror. Terror tactics result in a vicious circle where the innocent suffer on both sides.
We believe in the right of Israel to exist in security. We also believe in the right of the Palestinians to a homeland. Let Canadian and world opinion say very clearly that neither of these worthy goals can be achieved through the use of terrorism.
In the meantime, we join with those families and friends who hope and pray for a safe and peaceful outcome of the present crisis.

Mr. Speaker, the performance of the Canadian economy has been ever more promising since the election of the Conservative Government: close to 340,000 new jobs have been created, unemployment has gone down 1.5 per cent, inflation has been under 4 per cent over the past year, thus creating the most stable climate of confidence since 1971, and the real GNP has been rising at an annual rate of 4.1 per cent.
October 9, 1985

Indeed our performance since last year has been second to none among the seven major industrialized countries, and the confidence of investors over the past four years has been at an unprecedented level. The Bank of Canada rate has dropped from 12.38 to 8.99 per cent. The chartered banks' prime rate has decreased from 13 to 10 per cent, the lowest level in seven years. During the first eight months of 1985 bankruptcies declined by 13 per cent, retail sales rose by 10 per cent, motor vehicle sales were up by 23 per cent, the value of building permits is 17 per cent higher, and oil drilling activities have expanded by 19 per cent over the same period last year. The performance of the Canadian economy has also outranked that of the United States. The GNP and the net disposable income of individuals has grown twice as fast in Canada as in the United States.
I must inform the Hon. Member that his time has expired. The Hon. Member for Beauce (Mr. Bernier).

subsubtopic: BEAUCE EXAMPLE FOR REST OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, aside from the negative comments being made by the Opposition and a number of insinuations that do not always reflect the truth, the Member for Beauce (Mr. Bernier) is delighted to see that increasingly, one can rely on Canadians to improve our economy. I am proud to mention, in this respect, the example being set by my riding for the rest of Canada.
One company, Les systemes Archimede in Saint-Frederic, signed a $6 million contract last Friday with France for the construction of 1670 modular housing units for two French villages. The company, which now employs 20 people, will increase its establishment to 90 permanent employees. Last year the company, which was established in 1981, grossed $1.3 million. This year, it expects that figure to be $8 million, and in four years probably $ 12 million.
The phenomenal growth of this company in the Beauce area which has already obtained international recognition, is due to the dynamic and constant efforts being made by its leaders, and that applies to many other companies in my riding. It is time for us to exploit our strengths, our potential and our skills to improve the economy of our country. The people in the towns and villages of Beauce have realized this and are acting accordingly.
In Beauce, we are not interested in so-called scandals and negative articles in the media. We are intent on improving the well-being of the people, and our energies are dedicated to economic development.

subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF OAKVILLE SHOE MANUFACTURING PLANT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one week ago Susan Shoe Industries of Hamilton announced the closure of its Oakville plant and the permanent lay-off of 100 employees. The decision to close this plant was directly linked to the failure of the Mulroney Government to state its policy on the extension of footwear quotas.
After the closure was announced, Susan Shoe arranged a meeting in Ottawa with its Member of Parliament and the political Minister for the Hamilton area. The owner of Susan Shoe had arranged to travel from Montreal, the president of the Canadian Union was to travel from New York, and the other company officials were to travel from Hamilton.
Yesterday, the office of the Hon. Member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek) informed Susan Shoe officials that this meeting would have to be cancelled due to an urgent family commitment which would entail a trip to Toronto. Imagine the surprise, Mr. Speaker, when the Hon. Member for Halton, the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport and Minister of State for Multiculturalism, was spotted at last night's Blue Jay game sitting smiling behind the Prime Minister. Amid cries of "tuna, tuna, tuna" at Exhibition Stadium, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport were striking out on the Government's promise of "jobs, jobs, jobs."
When is the Government going to start demonstrating some concern for Canada's footwear industry? While the Blue Jays won last night, the Hon. Member for Halton lost the respect of workers in Canada's footwear industry.

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the document that I have just tabled is more than a comprehensive response to the second and third reports of the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons. It is a commitment fulfilled and a challenge issued.
During the last election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made the commitment that the reform of Canada's central institutions of Government would be an early priority of his administration. The Prime Minister's objective was to ensure that Government became more open and responsive to the views and requirements of all Canadians.

It is not surprising that in the Speech from the Throne at the opening of this Parliament the Government advocated various mechanisms to set in motion the process of a detailed review of the Government's machinery. One of its initiatives was to propose the creation of a Special Committee on Reform of the House of Commons.

Under the invaluable leadership of the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), the other members of the committee, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault), the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis), the Hon. Member for Peace River (Mr. Cooper) and the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) worked together in a spirit of non-partisan co-operation that stands as a model for our deliberations in this House and its committees.
The Special Committee rose to the challenge given to it in its broad mandate and produced three substantive reports containing a wide range of proposals for reform. Those proposals touched on matters as diverse as the role of the private
Statements by Ministers
Member and the modernization of the procedure governing the granting of Royal Assent.
Both in the comprehensive response to the first report which I tabled last April and in the response which I have just tabled, the Government's appreciation of the substantial support for the committee's recommendations is evident. However, I would like to take this opportunity on behalf of the Government to express once again our sincere appreciation to the Hon. Member for St. John's East-

maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD REPORTS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: REFORM OF THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
subtopic: SECOND AND THIRD REPORTS OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE-STATEMENT OF PRESIDENT OF THE PRIVY COUNCIL
speechtext:
-and indeed to all the other members of the committee for their hard work and their excellent results. 1 am sure all Members of the House, as they have indicated by their applause today, join with me in that sincere expression of thanks.
Eleven months have now passed since the Speech from the Throne. In that period, the Government has taken several important steps to further the process of parliamentary reform. From the very first, the Government recognized the importance of parliamentary scrutiny and input into major policy initiatives and substantially increased the number of policy statements delivered by Ministers in the House. In June, I tabled a discussion paper which proposed a major change in the legislation governing the redistribution of electoral boundaries. That paper was referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections and, pursuant to the recommendations of that committee, legislation is now before the House, legislation which if passed, will limit the future growth of the House and thereby ensure that each Member has greater access to the time of the House and its committees. This is an important step because the special committee has called for smaller standing committees and this proposal can only be met in a House that is at or only slightly larger than its present size. [Translation]
In addition, the Government has taken another step to bring Parliament closer to modern times by introducing legislation which acknowledges the supremacy of Parliament but which, for the first time ever, gives collective bargaining rights to House of Commons and Senate employees.

Furthermore, following the tabling of the Government's response to the first report of the special committee, the House agreed to adopt on a trial basis the vast majority of the reforms proposed in that report. As a result, the House is now experimenting with the following: one, extension of hours for ministerial statements; two, legislative committees; three, committee budgets; and four, a new, more meaningful Board of Internal Economy.

Last July the Prime Minister announced the establishment of a sub-committee of the Committee on Priorities and Planning to consider the question of the reform of the House. During the summer my colleagues and I examined the sugges-

October 9, 1985
Statements by Ministers
tions of the Special Committee on Reform to ensure the orderly implementation of reforms.

Today the Government has provided its response to the Second and Third reports of the special committee. In that response, we have not only indicated our support for the vast majority of the proposals contained in those reports but have, in the spirit of those reports, gone further to recommend additional measures designed to enhance or restore the role and authority of the House of Commons. For example, whereas the special committee proposed that standing committees of the House be given authority to review certain limited classes of Order in Council appointments, the Government's response goes far beyond that proposal. As the Prime Minister announced a few weeks ago, although committees will not be given the power to veto appointments, they will have the authority to review all Order in Council appointments. Furthermore, in the case of appointments to quasi-judicial bodies, committees will have the right to call nominees prior to their appointment.
This tendency to build upon the foundations laid out in the second and third reports can be found throughout our response. Indeed, Sir, it is our hope that reform will be a living and continuing process in this House. To accomplish that goal, however, we need to ensure that adequate consultation takes place between the Parties and that achievable, short-term objectives are set. It is for that reason that I have already met with my colleagues across the aisle to discuss these reforms. In fact, several of the Government responses have been adjusted to accommodate the views and suggestions of Opposition House Leaders.
In the coming weeks, I will be meeting with my counterparts again to ensure that the vigorous start which the House has made is carried forward and sees the development of a new House of Commons in the near future. Without prejudging the outcome of those discussions, it would be my hope that the reforms now before the House could be in place by the time Parliament reassembles next January.
The reforms we have proposed in our response, along with the several related initiatives such as regulation of activity by lobbyists, will shape our agenda for action in the coming months and years. This is an evolutionary change, but an important one.

The ultimate assessment of the strength of our democracy rests on the ability of our institutions and of all Canadians to face that challenge: as parliamentarians we will not be judged by what we do today but, in the long run, by our ability to make the institution efficient and relevant to society and its future needs.

In closing, let me call upon all of my colleagues in the House to take up the courageous road which will lead to a
better House, a more effective and democratic institution and the best possible forum to ensure that our great diversity can be given legitimate expression in unity of purpose. That is our commitment and our challenge.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of my parliamentary House Leader, I rise to speak on behalf of my party in reply to the Minister's statement, and considering the fact that I was advised on very short notice, not more than an hour ago, I trust the House will bear with me if I do not cover all the questions or points raised by the Minister.
That being said, we are delighted with this opportunity to join the Minister in congratulating once again the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) who provided the leadership on the Committee, with, of course, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and occasionally, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner).

The work done by the committee will be helpful to us all. 1 only wish the Government had taken most, if not all, its recommendations into serious consideration.

Mr. Speaker, the statement by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn) on the Government's comprehensive response to the Second and Third Reports of the Special Committee on Reform of the House of Commons seems incomplete, since it fails to mention that the practice of responding to committee reports was started during the last Parliament, on the initiative of the Liberal Government of the day, to enable committees to have more impact and to receive more comprehensive responses to their reports from the Government.
Mr. Speaker, parliamentary reform is only acceptable if it is the result of a consensus reached by all parties. It is never acceptable if it is treated as a partisan issue. To have a consensus, any parliamentary reform must first be shown to have as its objective the strengthening of the democratic process, not just increasing the authority of a Government that is already too powerful, as we see it.

As an example of how Government can try to smuggle in measures of advantage to it cloaked in the guise of non-partisan reform, we see in the Minister's statement a glowing reference to his redistribution Bill. The Minister should know that the jury is still out on that measure and that there are very serious doubts in the country about how that Bill may dilute even further the principle of one man, one vote. He should know that that measure is being looked at very skeptically and that he has yet to persuade the country that it is a reform of a positive nature.

October 9, 1985
Similarly, he should know that the proposals for procedural reform will be looked at with a skeptical eye. For example, the proposal for review of appointees looks very much like a paper tiger, an expression I like to use. However, in this case I think it would be more appropriate to say that it looks like a paper tiger without teeth. The Government has yet to provide details on how it sees the system working. More important, it does not propose that' committees reviewing appointments can do anything substantial about the bad choices which this Government makes. It borrows from the American system and says that all Order in Council appointments will be reviewed by the committee. The Government knows that the committee cannot do that. It is somewhat like saying that no right of veto will be accorded to committees. It is a paper tiger without teeth.

Now that the Government is proposing to adopt a broader set of reforms, Mr. Speaker, I can promise you that the Opposition will monitor very closely and critically the specific proposals that are being made.
For instance, in the comprehensive response tabled by the Government, we see a promise to agree to extend consideration of the Estimates by committees, accompanied by a condition that can or could make this reform totally meaningless.
I am thinking especially about the critical question of whether Members of Parliament should be independent from the Government when they sit in a committee or whether we should at least try to make them more indepedent. Recommendation 4.5 of the Committee states that if we want to reduce the size of standing committees and make them more independent, parliamentary secretaries should no longer sit on them.
The Government has rejected this proposal, even though we are trying to give more independence and powers to the committees. The Government insists that the parliamentary secretary, who is the assistant of the Minister, must be a member of the committee. Contrary to the committee recommendation to the effect that there be only seven members per committee, the Government says that there must be eight and adds the parliamentary secretary. I do not find this very serious, Mr. Speaker.

The entire tone of the response of the Government is, in my opinion, "If it helps us, we will do it. If it does not help us, we will see. If it slows us down, forget it". In its discussions with the opposition Parties, a greater disposition toward compromise and toward truly meaningful reform will be required of this Government.
In the brief period since the recommendations of the first report of the committee have been adopted on an experimental basis, we have already seen some areas where further adjustment will be needed.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note that the Government accepted the recommendations of the first report, but on an experimental basis, without getting away from the main issue. However, as far as the recommendations contained in the second and third reports are concerned, the Government has asked for more advantages before even putting these recommendations to the test.
Mr. Speaker, we plan on meeting soon with the Government Members and the Members of the New Democratic Party to discuss the important issue of reform. We congratulate once more the committee and its chairman for having discussed the matter objectively and for making special efforts to achieve a parliamentary consensus on the whole issue of reform.
We give notice to the Government that the only road to progress in parliamentary reform is to look for a consensus amongst all interested parties.
Mr. Speaker, I shall close by congratulating once more the committee and by asking this House to guarantee the independence of the committees and to examine closely and seriously the recommendations of the committee on reform, which I consider very serious and worthy of being implemented.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not be very long in dealing with this matter because it will be dealt with in much more detail some time later on. 1 wish to take a moment or two to make some points on matters which I think are quite important.
At the outset, I wish to congratulate the committee for its work, as did the Government House Leader and others. I know from my own experience how hard the Chairman of the committee and members of the committee have worked. I also know that it was able to do what many committees of the House of Commons are not able to do and, in fact, it was able to do what the House itself is unable to do, that is to say, work by consensus. As time passes, I hope that experience will rub off and that other Members of the House will recognize that it is better in the long run with respect to most issues to attempt to find a consensus than it is to push everyone to the wall on everything which is placed before us. Thus, I congratulate the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath).
I also wish to say to him that the reports over which he has presided are, in my judgment, a great move forward in the modernization of the parliamentary system. Wherever we do have disagreements-and there are two or three areas which are up for further discussion, I can say on my own behalf, and, I hope, on behalf of the others, that we will attempt on every occasion to come down four square alongside the committee. We believe that the committee did its work and did it well. I say that to all members of the committee.
There are two or three matters which puzzled me a little. These are matters which could be, perhaps, reviewed again. I

October 9, 1985
Statements by Ministers
note with interest that the Government House Leader has indicated that that in fact will be the process.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure the Hon. Member who chaired the committee knows, the House Leaders have in fact met on a number of occasions and have gone through the recommendations. They have looked at methods of implementation, taking into account certain of the problems which arise which have to be resolved in advance of implementation. And I am confident that over the course of the next two or three weeks, certainly in advance of the opening of the next session of this Parliament, we will have these rules in place, as we have all of the other recommendations in place which the committee recommended to the House.
I do, however, want to suggest one matter which is of major concern to me, that is, the recommendation which dealt with the question of petitions. There was a recommendation which I cannot quote verbatim but which I can paraphrase. The recommendation was that it would require a minimum of 25 persons in order to constitute a legally acceptable petition. I suggest that that is a dangerous precedent. I do think that it is the right of every individual citizen to petition his or her Parliament, and that has been the basis upon which the system has grown. If there is but one citizen someplace who feels aggrieved by the actions of his Parliament or by the results of the actions of his Parliament, he has the inalienable right to bring forward a petition and seek redress. I would be reluctant to go from that which I consider to be a very good principle to a principle which requires that a person have the support of 25 other persons in order to petition. I do not see that that is absolutely essential.
It does not seem to be too terribly onerous in a country which has a population of 25 million to find 25 persons to agree on one matter. However, a matter which is being brought to the attention of Parliament could well be a matter which affects one person directly or it may be matter about which one person feels particularly strongly. So I think I would, perhaps, beg of the House that at some point we not accept that change, well intentioned though it may be, and that we leave it as a right of every citizen to petition his or her Parliament in his or her own name asking for redress. I feel that that would make sense.
Another matter I would like to raise is one with which I know we are going to deal. We have had conversation about it and although it does not appear in the response of the Government, I am confident it is going to be dealt with when we sit down to discuss methods of implementation. It is the whole question of the numbers and definitions of committees. The Government House Leader will recall when he, the House Leader for the Official Opposition and myself gathered together one week ago tonight in the Commonwealth room to welcome a significant number of representatives of the ethnic communities of Canada as they celebrated the establishment of the ethnocultural committee. That is the committee which looks at questions directly related to ethnicity and the development of Canada in the future. We all said the same thing, that
this was a much needed, long postponed initiative on the part of Government and on the part of Parliament.
It would seem passing strange that we should, one week later, indicate to that group that we do not think it is necessary, but I do not believe that that was the intent of the Government House Leader-in fact, I know it was not. It was only after consultation with him that I decided to raise this question. I believe that he and I both agree, as does the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), the House Leader for the Official Opposition, that there will be the necessity to add committees, albeit a few, to the list of committees recommended by the Committee on Reform of the House of Commons for the very reason that there are certain things which we all deem to be necessary and certainly advisable, and we should bear in mind that those committees may well have to be included, along with the others.
So I say to those who are in the ethnic community in Canada today, and who travelled all the way to Ottawa to join with us in celebrating the establishing of the committee: Fear not, it is not going to be done away with. We have already agreed to it.
As far as the balance of the recommendations are concerned, I say as delicately as I can to the Speaker that regarding recommendation No. 73, which indicates the Speaker's power to select, as well as to combine amendments at the report stage-I recognize that this is a power the Speaker has, and I say this not necessarily for the incumbent but for the future reference of others who might not be as attuned to the system as it now exists-in that selection process, great care should be exercised, if it were in fact to be utilized, to ensure that in that selection process the subject matter of the amendments are also taken into account. Not only would they have to be admissible in a technical sense but the subject matter, those areas to which the amendments address themselves, must in fact be appropriately addressed in some other way in determining whether or not there could be the removal of one or more amendments offered at the report stage to be selected by the Speaker.
In addition to that, we must recognize the political nature of the House of Commons. It may well be that for crass political reasons-and I know that rarely do we ever do anything for those reasons-it is necessary to pay recognition to the fact of whether an amendment came from the Government'side of the House or from the opposition side of the House and, even more important, I believe, whether it came from the two opposition Parties jointly. In all fairness, it may be necessary to recognize that both opposition Parties have submitted similar amendments in order that both can claim credit for having pushed the Government right to the wall-which is always what we are trying to do, in any event.
I realize you might find that hard to believe, Mr. Speaker, but I am prepared to admit it because there is not another soul in the world watching this. They are all watching the Blue Jays. I feel quite confident that I can say almost anything today. There is not a single person watching us on television, I am sure. Everyone is sitting watching the Blue Jays, and at the
October 9, 1985

end of the first half of the first inning, they are tied nothing each.
I am confident that we will get these changes into being by the first part of January and that we will see them working. It will not be easy. Change is difficult and we have just made some changes and I hear nothing but complaints about the way these changes are affecting people's lives. That does not mean the changes are wrong. It just means that politicians, by their very nature, resist change. That seems to be the case even with the changes to the House of Commons. However, may 1 say that I am looking forward to helping to implement these changes and to making sure we get the best possible results from what I consider to be an absolutely excellent series of recommendations made by a committee which worked diligently on behalf of all of us.

speechtext: May I advise the House that because of the ministerial statement, consideration of Government Orders will be extended by 27 minutes this day.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. McDougall that Bill C-79, an Act respecting the provision of compensation to depositors of Canada Commercial Bank, CCB Mortgage Investment Corporation and Northland Bank in respect to uninsured deposits, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra) (p. 7379).

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to speak in support of Bill C-79, which concerns the provision of compensation to depositors of the two financial institutions, for the portion not insured by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. The Bill was tabled by the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) in the House on October 7 of this year.
Through this Bill, the Government intends to compensate all depositors who had invested their savings with the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, and who would not otherwise have been compensated by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. Last March, when the Government
took emergency action to improve the financial situation of these institutions located in Western Canada, it made certain commitments to the depositors of these institutions, and today, it intends to meet those commitments. Last March we had created a climate of trust in these institutions, but repeated attacks by the Opposition created a climate of panic and uncertainty in the financial world, especially among small depositors and business people. Mr. Speaker, how can the Government be expected to build something solid when the Opposition, in an unprecedented way and without consideration, is constantly undermining the commitment we made to preserve those financial institutions, together with many private depositors and small businessmen, over six major chartered banks and the provincial Governments that were directly concerned. Today, we must meet the commitments we made to these people. They trusted us, and thanks to the criticism by Opposition Members, today they might have lost everything. We are going to meet our obligations to the bitter end, and the Opposition should do likewise and support the Bill, since it would not have been necessary without the Opposition's attacks on the bail-out program we proposed last March, and the consequences of those attacks. In fact, why did these financial institutions have to close their doors? I will try to define several significant developments these institutions have had to deal with in recent years.
First, the energy policy of our predecessors, who today are the Official Opposition, has had a disastrous impact on Western Canada, and it is in fact Western Canada, Mr. Speaker, which has been most severely affected by the failure of these financial institutions. The Liberal Government took a series of energy measures which resulted in a dramatic drop in oil consumption, and these measures included energy transfer policies such as programs to help people convert from oil heating to electricity and also increased taxes in this sector.
Second, rising interest rates which our predecessors merely encouraged, plus inflation which they were unable to control, both led Canadians to review their consumption habits, such as gas for motor vehicles, and so forth. This dangerous legacy we were left by the previous Government is now forcing us to take the measures before the House today. The Opposition, the Liberals, did not foresee the consequences of their actions at the time they took these economic initiatives, as a result of which today, so many people in Western Canada are facing serious economic problems.
And now, Mr. Speaker, what about the regulation of our financial institutions? As soon as it came to power last September, our Government asked for a major review of our financial institutions, since we were aware of the disastrous consequences of the regulations left to us by the previous Government. Mr. Speaker, as you know, only a few months ago we referred a green paper to the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, for the purpose of assessing the consequences of poor regulation of these financial institutions.
October 9, 1985

Last summer we heard evidence from spokesmen for most banks, trust and insurance companies to launch a basic reform to avoid the reoccurrence of such incidents in the future.
Our only regret-and there is nothing we could do about it-is that we did not come into office a year sooner, for we certainly would have been able to avoid the shutdown of the two Canadian banks which are now the subject matter of this Bill. As a result of those policies, both banks-the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank-had to cope with all kinds of problems. Unemployment increased, the market value of real estate declined, and the special nature of mortgage legislation resulted in those two institutions finding themselves stuck with boxes full of keys to houses on which they held mortgages. Homeowners were no longer able to meet their obligations. In turn the banks were unable to meet theirs.
That sums up the reasons which explain how Western Canada found itself in the midst of an economic crisis. Since we are a national Government we have to lend a hand to a region of our country, Western Canada, which finds itself in dire straits. Our duty is to help that region solve the problems it is facing. More than that, we have to assess the consequences of our action if we were to refuse to help the depositors of those two financial institutions which are now in the process of being liquidated.
Private individuals had deposits of about $27 million in the two banks, and I would suggest we cannot let them fend for themselves because there are too many of them. Nor can we forget the unions and their deposits of about $7 million. As we all know union funds come mostly from low wage workers. Are we going to ignore all those small depositors?
The problem is the same when it comes to municipalities: if we do nothing about their deposits we will be asking small depositors, people who must pay taxes on their homes, to bear the brunt of this whole affair, and we are talking about roughly $82 million.
Credit unions are in the same predicament. Religious organizations stand to lose close to $22 million. If one remembers that the money was collected cent by cent, one can imagine just how many people are involved. We cannot ignore those organizations for the sake of $22 million and it is imperative that we continue to protect them. Pension funds and small businessmen account for an additional $6 million, so all told we are looking at about $230 million which directly affect individuals in a relatively small region.
What, then, would be the cost of the measures the government would have to take in this area if we did not compensate them now? It would have to help them directly or indirectly through various social schemes, including unemployment insurance and welfare programs, which would probably cost a lot more than what we are giving now.
We can imagine what loss in income tax the government would incur if we abandoned these people to their own
Depositors Compensation
resources, for small businesses would probably have to close and the Government would lose major fiscal revenues; $230 million for those who have adhered to our bailout package, that is very little.
In other words, what would be the price we would have to pay to rebuild this region which is the most severely affected by these bank failures and to ensure the economic future of its people?
The $875 million provided for under this Bill is certainly a large amount of money, but it is not much in term of helping these people to operate in a recovering economy. The economic policies implemented by our Government over the past few months have already made possible the creation of some 284,000 jobs; what is more, a large number of foreign corporations which have confidence in our economy are currently negociating possible investments in Canada, which should create hundreds of thousands new jobs in this country. Also we should not forget that our policies for the past year only have reduced unemployment by 1.5 per cent to restore the steadiest climate since 1971: bank rates have been greatly reduced, automobile plants have increased their production by 23 per cent, construction has increased by 17 per cent. And if we specifically refer to the West, oil drilling companies have increased their operations by 19 per cent.
It was for all those reasons that I mentioned a while ago that if we had had the opportunity to come to power a year earlier, we would not have experienced all those consequences. We do not want to bail out the bank or the financial institution as suggested by the Opposition. They alter the facts. It is far more dramatic not to compensate the small businessmen and the ordinary Canadians who have so painfully saved.
We may not be happy today to have to pay out such a sum. However, we have to do so to protect and maintain the parliamentary spirit. It is due to the irresponsibility of the previous government that we have to pay and Canadians know it, they are not easily deceived. They know that we are paying for the administrative mistakes of the team now sitting opposite.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I support this Bill as a responsible parliamentarian and all parliamentarians either on the Government side or in the Opposition should do likewise.

speechtext: Order. Are there comments or questions on the Hon. Member's speech? If not, we will resume debate with the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau).

Mr. Speaker, 1 heard the comments made by the Hon. Member who spoke before me. He referred to the reasons why the Government stepped in and introduced this legislation. And like all Conservative Members, he was anxious to put the blame on the previous Government.

October 9, 1985
