However, Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Member for Longueuil (Mr. Leblanc) had taken the time to read the statmenet made by the Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) in this House on March 25th, certainly he would have changed his speech, because according to a Member of this Conservative Government the Canadian Commercial Bank's difficulties were due: "to the Canadian Commercial Bank's operations in the United States and the losses incurred in the United States by that bank".
Moreover, for the benefit of the Hon. Member for Longueuil, I am going to quote what the Minister, a Conservative Minister in his Government, had to say in this House, and since I have the English text, he will allow me to read it in English. Mrs. McDougall had this to say:
The bank recently experienced a sharp deterioration in its U.S. loan portfolio, particularly as a result of lower oil prices. This situation significantly depressed the value of the Canadian Commercial Bank loan portfolio.

If I understand correctly the comments made by the Minister on March 25, 1985, when she announced that the Canadian Commercial Bank was having difficulties, I believe these were in the nature of the difficulties known to exist in the United States rather than difficulties facing the Canadian economy in western Canada. For sure, if the Minister who is now on the spot wants to change the speech she made on March 25, she will give us the reasons. But one thing is certain. If the Hon. Member for Longueuil (Mr. Leblanc) had read that statement made by his colleague, a Minister of his Government, he would not have made such comments.
Mr. Speaker, when dealing with Bill C-79 I have the feeling I am taking part in a demolition project, the demolition of two financial institutions, and the demolition of something which was certainly part of the pride shared by Canadians living in the Prairies and Western Canada. Because this Bill is the death sentence passed on two financial institutions, two regional banks which operated in Western Canada, even though they had operations elsewhere in this country.
What the Government is proposing is using the taxpayers' money to actually cover that part of the assets of those two banks which was in trouble. It is clear to me, according to the statements we heard from Government Members, that the cost-it is not yet known and I will come back to this-will be based on the amount of bad loans and the ability of liquidators to get the best price possible for the assets. I will also come back to this later, and refer to the Hitchman Report which seems to indicate that the Government, faced with the options outlined by the expert, chose the one that was least recommended by Mr. Hitchman himself.
What this demolition project undertaken by Bill C-79 boils down to, is that the overall cost to the Government and its
agencies totals $3.3 billion. In the case of the Northland Bank, it is first a sum of $1,232 billion, which breaks down into $414 million for uninsured deposits, $318 million for insured deposits and a $500 million advance from the Bank of Canada, for a total cost of $1,232 billion with respect to just one bank.
In the case of the Canadian Commercial Bank, there will be an expenditure of $2 billion, of which $532 million will be for uninsured deposits, $275 million for insured deposits and $1.3 billion for the money advanced by the Bank of Canada, for a total of $3,332 billion.
This is a substantial amount, and it will come either from the Government directly through this bill or from the Bank of Canada, which will try to recover its losses. Whatever amount the Bank of Canada succeeds in recovering will lower the amount that the Government can recover under Bill C-79, and whether we want it or not, there will also be the amounts paid by the CDIC, which will be passed on to consumers. Instead of being a tax to be paid at income tax time, this will be passed on as additional costs for banking operations throughout the system.
What will be the real cost of this operation? That is the question, Mr. Speaker. Until now, a figure of $1 billion has been quoted. In other words, after the Government has recovered whatever it can, the net cost would be about $1 billion. For those who have examined the Hitchman Report which was tabled this morning-and I am pleased that it has finally been made public after we had been asking for it such a long time- I can point out that this report states on page 6 that the necessary reserves for bad loans in the case of the Canadian Commercial Bank would be of $1 billion. This is only for one bank. If the report is true, the cost will be $1 billion for a single bank.
How much will it cost for the Northland Bank? We do not know yet, but apparently, it will certainly be around $225 million, which means that the real cost to the Crown will not be $1 billion as we had thought until now, but more like $1.2 billion.
Mr. Speaker, we have asked the Minister of State for Finance and the Minister of Finance, who has the ultimate responsibility for the financial administration of this country, to provide clarification about the real cost of this operation. However, in her comments last Monday, the Minister of State for Finance candidly admitted that she had no real idea of the true cost to the taxpayers, but she certainly did not deny that this cost would exceed $1 billion.
I do not want to go over the entire speech that I made in this House during the special debate on the Northland Bank which the Chair granted to us some days ago, more specifically last week, I believe. At that time, we thought that the Minister would rise to inform us about what was happening to the second bank facing financial problems. However, nothing happened; the Minister spoke for about 20 minutes, and during all that time, she succeeded in evading the issue completely and
October 9, 1985

not saying a word about the Northland Bank. Because of that, we now have no information about this financial institution. We simply know what the newspapers have reported and what we have learned in our conversations with certain officials, which is very little. Yet, the Members of Parliament are being asked to approve a Bill which requests hundreds of millions of dollars, to be paid by the Canadian taxpayers.
Hon. Members will recall that during the emergency debate, the Government was asked some very specific questions, and in particular why the Department of Finance had decided to tie together the fates of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, which amounted to giving the latter the kiss of death, and in fact simply forced it to close its doors.
Why are we now discussing Bill C-79? Why is the Government now being forced to introduce a Bill dealing with nearly $1 billion? I suggest that the basic reason goes back to last March, when the Government made a commitment, and assured the House and the people of Canada that the bail-out which was being attempted by putting up $255 million for the Canadian Commercial Bank was going to be a success, that the Bank was going to become solvent again and that depositors were not to have any fears of leaving their deposits in that financial institution of Western Canada.
Some of my constituents, Mr. Speaker, had deposits in the Canadian Commercial Bank which came due in April, one month after the bail-out operation, and hesitated to renew those deposits. They phoned the Bank of Canada, and I have the number they dialed, I even have the name of the person they talked to, and that person told them: "If you do not trust the Canadian Commercial Bank, you might as well not go to any bank at all, for they are all alike". This is the information that was given to one of my constituents who phoned the Bank of Canada to find out if the Canadian Commercial Bank was safe. The officer involved was of course not providing an answer on the basis of his own knowledge, he was passing on the Government's message, he was to all intents and purposes repeating the statements made by the Minister of Finance, the Minister of State for Finance, the Prime Minister, the Inspector of Banks and the Governor of the Bank of Canada.
Consciously or unconsciously, whether it wanted it or not, the Government misled depositors in this country who were dealing with this financial institution. They were giving information on the basis of data that were inadequate and incomplete. And now the Minister of Finance, the Minister of State (Finance) and the Prime Minister are obliged to make amends for their oversight and incompetence and to ask this House for authority to spend nearly one billion dollars to compensate depositors. It is because the Conservative Government gave false indications that taxpayers are now obliged to pay the bill. Is it normal that all Canadian taxpayers should be asked to pay for the incompetence and nonchalance of a Conservative Government that last March was more concerned with publicity, with the coverage of the Economic Summit when the Prime
Depositors Compensation
Minister sat on his television commentator's throne in front of Canada's business and labour world? Of course he did not want to give Canadians the bad news that a bank was going to go bankrupt. However, this desire on the part of the Prime Minister to play to the media led him to make a decision in a few hours, and the papers amply documented the process and the sequence of events to make them plausible for the public.
So a decision was made in a few minutes to avoid casting a pall on the Economic Summit, and today, the Government has to make amends and ask the House to consider a Bill that will total expenditures of nearly $1 billion. This is entirely inconceivable and irresponsible!
Mr. Speaker, today we are being asked to consider a very important Bill. In fact I do not think that within our lifetime as parliamentarians, in this Parliament, at least not until the next election, we will again be asked to vote on a Bill whose sole purpose is to spend $1 billion. It is not a social program, it is not an economic development program but just a Bill involving nearly one billion dollars.
In my view, to ask us to do that without having Mr. Justice Estey's report, to ask us to pass a piece of legislation without any indication of the causes which brought about Northland Bank's financial difficulties, as to whether that bank actually is in difficulty or concerning other aspects of its financial statements-We are now asked, yes, the Minister has the gall to ask us to rush through this Bill involving $1 billion without any information, without any data concerning Mr. Justice Estey's report, without information on the Northland Bank, without any reasonably precise information as to the value of the assets of those banks. This, Mr. Speaker, I feel is unacceptable. Coming from a Government I find it amateurish, I find it shameful to ask representatives of the people to rush this through without the basic information needed to make a judgment.
Besides, they will not give us the names of the persons or institutions to whom the money would be paid. 1 totally support the views expressed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) when he introduced the amendment namely that the Bill should not... the principle itself should not be recognized and accepted by this House if we do not have full information, total information, about whom that kind of money is going to be paid to. I think this is the minimum that could be asked from a democratic institution such as this Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to recall that another reason why we are asked to pass this Bill today is the statement made by the Minister of State (Finance) on March 29, 1985. Because on March 29, we only knew about the case and situation of the Northland Bank and Members in this House then asked the Minister of State (Finance) whether other institutions were in trouble.

October 9, 1985
Depositors Compensation
The Minister had answered:
I would like to make it clear that other institutions are not being looked at under the circumstances that we are talking about now. I want that absolutely clear for the House, the people of Canada and the depositors in our financial institutions.

We had been told that no other financial institutions were in trouble. So depositors, businessmen, individuals, institutions and municipalities heard supposedly responsible people-at the very least accountable for managing public funds in this country-telling them that no other financial institutions were in a bind. Well, no wonder those institutions and those individuals continued to have faith in the Northland Bank! But now, on September 1, we find out that the Minister had not told us the truth. So today we are again forced to make up for a factual error or mismanagement, but whether we like it or not the ultimate result is the same for the taxpayers-they have to pick up the tab. They have to pick up the tab, Mr. Speaker, and there is something unfair in all this.
A few days we heard that another financial institution, Continental Trust-about which the Minister did not say a word either last March 29-has collapsed, or at least is being liquidated. The depositors? They can be found in every region of Canada even though this financial institution did most of its business in Ontario. Some of them live in Quebec City and they called me. Others are from the Montreal region and they too called me. Among others, I have received a call from Mr. Henri Jones of St-Sauveur who wants me to ask the Government to explain why the foreign banks will be reimbursed in the case of the Northland Bank and the CCB while the depositors are not being compensated in the case of the Continental Trust. How can this be logically explained?
Mr. Speaker, you are indicating that I have two minutes remaining. I shall have to condense my comments substantially. I would have liked to speak about the Hitchman Report, but as far as the Northland Bank is concerned and based on the recommendations contained in this report, I am asking the Government to postpone consideration of this Bill to see whether there would not be another solution to the problems of this bank.
I would like to suggest to the Government a four-part program the purpose of which would be to save the Northland Bank from liquidation and closure.
First, we know that the costs will be at least equal to the losses or bad loans. In one way and another, the costs will be approximately the same. Especially if we look at the Hitchman report, liquidation seems to be the least desirable solution when a bank is having this kind of problem.
First, therefore, if it is true that the potential losses exceed the assets of the shareholders in the case of the Northland
Bank, which means that the assets of the shareholders are zero, I would suggest that the Government purchase for SI and other considerations the assets of ordinary shareholders.
Second, the Government should introduce a special bill, different from this one-the money we are spending now will be lost entirely-to invest in the equity of the Northland Bank about as much as we will have to spend to cover the bad loans of the bank. How much would that cost? Between $150 million and $200 million. We are spending that much anyway.
Third, it should change, if need be, the composition of the board of directors and appoint, if necessary, a new and more competent team.
Fourth, it should guarantee the deposits in the Northland Bank for the next five years, so that depositors could regain confidence in this financial institution.
The purpose of this four-point strategy would be to bail out the Northland Bank at a cost to the Canadian taxpayers, based again on the recommendations of the Hitchman report, which would be a lot lower than the current liquidation of the assets.
This way, we would undoubtedly save money, we would at least keep some people at work and probably save for Western Canada a financial institution which did not deserve to fail.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments on the Hon. Members remarks? Debate. The Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-79 which is an Act respecting the provision of compensation to depositors of Canadian Commercial Bank, CCB Mortgage Investment Corporation and Northland Bank in respect of uninsured deposits.
I believe that when all the facts are known, when cool rational judgment prevails, the decision to assist the uninsured depositors in these financial institutions will be seen as being fair, based on all the facts that were available at that time, based upon the unique situation at that time-and I will deal with that point in a little more detail-based on the competence of the individuals who were giving information, and based on the honesty of the individuals who were giving information at that time.
I would just like to quote from the Financial Times of October 7 of this week. It says:
The Mulroney Government's decision to create a commission of inquiry to look into the failures of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank makes good sense. In fact, it will be downright healthy to remove the banking fiasco from the House of Commons, where the matter is getting blurred instead of clarified with each passing day.
In appointing Supreme Court Judge Willard Estey to head the commission, Prime Minister Brian Mulroney said "the factors affecting the situation of the two banks are complex and require thorough and dispassionate analysis."
October 9, 1985

It has become increasingly-sometimes alarmingly-clear in the weeks since the banks' critical conditions became known that neither Parliament nor a parliamentary committee would be likely to deliver the kind of "dispassionate analysis" the whole matter is begging for.
The objectives of the decision included the very strong and supportive ideal to nurture and foster the development of regional banks. Also they included the need to maintain confidence in the banking system. We have a record which is well worth defending, going back some 62 years or 63 years. As Hon. Members know, one has to be very careful in pulling the plug, so to speak, on a financial institution. It can cause a domino effect which not only ripples through the financial factor but comes down very hard on small businesses. The bottom line in terms of the total impact upon Canada could be a tremendous loss of jobs. We have a record worth protecting. I believe the record will show that we tried to act in fairness to thousands of average Canadians. These Canadians, either directly or indirectly, had a stake in the confidence of the CCB and Northland. However, as I indicated already, Mr. Justice Willard Estey has been asked to look into all aspects of the collapse of these two banks. We are hopeful-in fact, we know it because of his competence-that he will explore in depth many roles-those of the external auditors, the Inspector General of Banks, the board of directors, the audit committees of the board of directors, the senior management of the company and the government officials, both at the federal level and at two provincial levels. He will also explore the loan practices, accounting practices, insider information and conflict of interest.
I was a member of the Finance Committee. We looked in some detail at the circumstances in May and June of this year, prior to the summer recess. Based upon the information which we were given-and we were refused certain documents-we had some very clear indication at that time that the renewing of bad loans and the advancing of more funds just to pay for past due interest was not a normal, sound practice. The practice of accruing interest when the principal was not even being paid and taking it into income was not sound. The practice of changing names on accounts just to renew the account and bring it into current standing was not correct. Adding substantial fees to the balance in renewing the account was not correct. Loans made to 100 per cent of the cost, in other words no equity whatsoever in the transaction, was not correct. Spreading the cost of the goodwill in connection with the purchase of the Westland Bank, which I recall was some $18.4 million, was intended to be spread over a 40-year period.
Possibly the record will show that all participants were misled in this situation. I am speaking about information being misleading, being faulty and being incomplete. If the true level of the assistance required was $255 million at that time, that bank would be thriving today. If criminal charges are warranted, I am sure they will be instituted. If other disciplinary action is necessary against organizations or individuals, that will be taken.
I should like to talk a little about the role and the importance of regional financial institutions. The Government believes in regional banks. They are of great benefit to local
Depositors Compensation
men and women as well as business people, particularly small business persons. Canada is dominated by five very large banks of world class size. In contrast, the United States of America has about 13,000 banks, partly as a result of the interstate banking regulations, but the situation in that country is far different from the one here. Our five large banks have something like 7,000 to 8,000 branches in Canada. Indeed, to start up a small regional bank is not an easy task. One of the principles of making loans is to spread risk. However, when one has started in a given region, obviously there will be some concentration in that local area. If the local area happens to have a concentration of energy industries, that also goes slightly against the risk factor. Those things have to be taken into consideration. There will be some ups and downs.
We feel it is very important, regardless of whether it is western Canada, Atlantic Canada or northern Ontario, to have regional banks. In 20 years or 30 years from now there should not be a total concentration in the financial industry by five or six very large conglomerates. Timing is also important, whether one is starting up a bank or any other type of business. Also there is a little luck involved. Of course luck can be good or it can be bad. In this particular case these institutions were just getting going when a very severe recession hit the country. That was compounded by developments in western Canada, particularly in Alberta. If only very large institutions survived, what would happen to competition and to pricing? I think some bad things could happen. We have seen some early indications. For example, a Minister of the Government of Alberta spoke on television this morning and indicated that some small and medium-sized borrowers were having difficulty borrowing funds.
I should like to talk about legislation for a moment. The Liberals discussed new legislation in 1982, but no concrete action was taken. The laws of the country governing the role of insurance companies and trust companies are some 50 years outdated. My Party, after forming the Government last fall, took action very quickly. A study was commissioned of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation; it is known as the Wyman Report. It was completed in April, 1985, and it is under review. A Green Paper was also commissioned by the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall). It included nine principles in total. It is very interesting that the first was: improve consumer protection; the second was; strictly control self dealing; the third was: guard against conflicts of interests; and the fourth was: promote competition and efficiency. There were several other key ones as well.
The revisions to The Bank Act in 1980 created a flood of new banks. The figure rose from something like 11 to 70. However, the former Government did absolutely nothing to improve supervisory control.
I should like to deal with the background of the Canadian Commercial Bank at this point. It received its charter in July, 1975. It started business in 1976, with the opening of two offices, one in Edmonton and one in Vancouver. It decided as a strategy to specialize in loans to small and medium-sized

October 9, 1985
Depositors Compensation
businesses in the energy service and real estate sectors. Its rate of growth is already on record.
I have already touched upon some of the risks facing new institutions in the growing stage. However, let me get right to the very serious decision in March, 1985. The federal Government agreed to a restructuring, but there were several other very competent, very able people at the table when that package was discussed. I refer, of course, to representatives from the Alberta Government who obviously wanted to see small banks survive, representatives of the Government of British Columbia, representatives of the CDIC, very senior officers from every one of the top six banks in this country, and representatives of the federal Government including the Governor of the Bank of Canada and the Inspector General of the Banks. They, in their wisdom, obtained all possible facts. As I recall, they began on a Friday evening. The deadline to make a decision was not three or six months away, it was that Monday morning.
I can still recall that the Chief Executive Officer of one of the large banks indicated at our hearings that, given the adequate, correct information available at that time, it was not unusual to make a decision of that type based on solid, hard, sound facts. Of course, part of that information is the valuation of loans, which is normally done in a competent way and over-viewed by external auditors from other areas.
There have been some hints, and I believe they are quite incorrect, that valuation is a relatively easy exercise. After all, the bank had something like 3,000 loan files. There are those who wonder why it could not have brought in 200 people to do these valuations on the weekend. It is not that simple, Mr. Speaker. Most lending officers with any experience would agree with me. One must be able to rely on the key people who supply information.
Let me give you a couple of examples of the difficulties involved in valuation, Mr. Speaker. Let us say that a file showed a piece of raw land as an asset. One cannot decide in one weekend exactly what that land is worth. It may be that it is abutting on a very profitable industrial development, but it may turn out that, according to the city plans, the trunk line sewers end there. If so, it is not going to be very valuable. In cases like that, one needs to know the city's development plans, the zoning of the property and how that property might be changed. The valuation of an industrial building, for example, cannot be determined by its number of square feet, number of bricks or tonnes of mortar. The value of a building like that is based upon the value of rentals and the cash flow. One has to have a very solid idea of the nature of the tenants and the expiry dates of leases to know what value could be placed on that building. The same criterion goes for equipment, whether it is oil rigs or construction equipment. To know the value, one must know things like the current contracts for the equipment and the income raised from those contracts. In summary, on the issue of valuation, any five experts in this country must rely upon the information they are given.
I submit that this decision had to be made in quick order. We are not discussing the possible closing of a Gulf refinery, something which one might take six months to discuss. Confidence is key to a financial institution. We could not expect to maintain confidence with people running around all over the place.
All the options were explored. I have already touched upon the people who were involved. They were very senior people and they came to a unanimous decision, based upon the information they had, to go ahead with this support package. Realizing the very unique circumstances that existed at that time and the difficult economic situation, they realized that they were dealing with the future and survival of regional banks. They also decided to try to find a marriage partner for the Northland Bank.
Once the decision was made, those involved had to speak with confidence from that point on. Some people have been critical of the statements of confidence made by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Minister of State for Finance and the Inspector General of Banks. Someone who would argue with that is someone who just does not know what he is talking about. Having made that decision, one does not begin to say, "I think that bank might survive", or "Maybe it will succeed". Once that decision has been made, those who have made the decision have to get behind it and do everything possible to support it.
I would like to touch briefly on the profile of the uninsured depositors. With the CCB, there were credit unions with deposits totalling $6.8 million. In other words, thousands of average Canadians had their savings in that institution. Municipalities had $41.1 million on deposit. Again at risk is the money of many Canadians. After all, a municipality receives its money through special surtaxes on property taxes or other measures. Shool boards had $3.1 million on deposit; religious organizations, $2.3 million; labour unions, $6.5 million; and hospitals, $5.2 million. The Northland Bank's depositor profile is very similar, except that charitable organizations had a total of $13.2 million on deposit.
Yes, many foreign banks were trying to help the institution survive. As well, some other large depositors were helping it to survive. We have asked members of the Opposition, without receiving any clear answer, what the criteria for choosing would be, if it would be valid to start to pick and choose which depositors should be saved, and I do not think it is valid.
Looking ahead, I think we need to get on with the new legislation, with dealing with the CDIC and with the reform of financial institutions. Clearly we must strengthen the supervisory role over banks. Clearly we must give the Minister more power to act when the alarm rings. That supervisory role has not been in place in a strong enough way.
Regarding the CDIC, we should decide what the limit of insurance should be. We need to decide if the limit should be greater than $60,000 and if there should be co-insurance. Dealing with the reform of financial institutions, there are many, many items with which we must come to grips. These include ownership limits, concentration of power, self-dealing,
October 9, 1985

conflicts of interest and leverage. Should all institutions be able to leverage 20 to one or higher? The role of the financial holding company, the role of Schedule C banks and the rest are all matters with which we must come to grips in order to put in place the mechanism that will establish on an ongoing basis a proper control of financial institutions so that we can return to making the record of which we in this country have been so proud for so many years.
In summary, I have made three points. First, I believe Bill C-79 should pass so that we may assist the many unions, school boards and municipalities that stood by this bank. Second, I think we should have confidence that Mr. Justice Estey's examination will determine all the facts and whether or not there was any wrongdoing. I think it was a great move to place the matter under his stewardship.
I would like to touch briefly on the important matter of privacy. I believe Mr. Justice Estey is the one who should decide on the matter of privacy. There is a law in this country that provides for privacy for both borrowers and depositors. I think it is critical that we maintain that. Mr. Justice Estey can look at the matter of privacy to help him determine if there was any wrongdoing, but I do not think we should see a knee-jerk reaction to a law that has been in place in Canada for over 100 years.
Finally, let us get on with revising the legislation regarding the CDIC. Let us get on with the reform of the regulations governing financial institutions to prevent the recurrence of situations like the one faced by the CCB and the Northland Bank.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) on his excellent contribution to this debate and also for his outstanding work on the Finance Committee. At the end of his remarks, he touched briefly on the matter of the privacy provisions and the revealing of the identities of depositors. My personal view is that to reveal those identities would cause irreparable damage to financial institutions because most people expect that their own names and the amounts of their deposits ought indeed to remain confidential. That is basic to our deposit-taking system. Would the Hon. Member care to comment with respect to the rationale behind the comments of those who would seek to apparently destroy those privacy provisions?

Mr. Speaker, I wish, through you, to thank the Hon. Member for his question. Privacy is critically important to all individual Canadians for a number of reasons. We need to have confidence in any dealings we have that they will remain private. We have laws under our Income Tax Act which state that no person, including Members of Parliament, is permitted to have access to the income tax files of an individual unless the individual says, in writing, that access is permissible. That is important.
Depositors Compensation
In the committee deliberations we spoke about the possible risks in this country of more and larger data banks being built. These data banks contain a great deal of personal information with respect to loans, income and other facts. We have some genuine concerns in this regard which will be dealt with in our recommendations with respect to tide selling, whether it is information passed on from magazine subscriptions or what have you. If these data bases contain critical information, and they will, which should be for the private and sole use of whatever individual institution the person has dealt with, be it a mortgage company or a bank, it should not be passed on the someone else. When individual Canadians take a loan from an institution, or when they make a deposit to an institution, they are doing so in keeping with the 100-year old tradition which says that if something is private it is private. Because of the regrettable problem, and it is regrettable, we should not break the principles of this long held tradition which is so important to so many Canadians.

On a comment, Mr. Speaker. I listened to the reply of the Hon. Member. I can only say that his argument with respect to privacy and confidentiality is fatuous in the extreme. We all recognize the right of confidentiality. However, when one comes to the Government of Canada and its taxpayers and asks for an ex gratia payment, is the Hon. Member saying that should be kept private? Surely, if one wants privacy and confidentiality then ones does not come with both hands out asking for an ex gratia payment. They can have their confidentiality but they will not receive their payment. They cannot have it both ways.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) wish to reply?

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member has missed the point. Confidentiality and privacy must be maintained. I wish to ask the Hon. Member this rhetorical question. What does he want the particular information for? I am strongly in support of Mr. Justice Estey having the complete information available to him so that, in his wisdom and with his legal advisers, he can decide if any wrongdoing has occurred. If there has been any wrongdoing, then let him proceed with alacrity and haste. However, I do not think that such private information should be within the purview of a 20-member committee of the House or any other group. We can look at the objectives with respect to why the Hon. Member may want to have some facts, but let us face them so that we can maintain the tradition while getting on with the purpose of why they may be interesting and available to use.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has not helped the situation at all. He is talking about the Parliament of Canada which is being asked to award unspecified amounts to unspecified persons or corporations and he dares to ask: Why does the Hon. Member want this information? It is as if the Hon. Member is someone who just wandered in from the street to see what was going on and was nosy about this particular issue. That is the Parliament of Canada. Parliament is being asked to award to people whom we do not know a total of more

October 9, 1985
Depositors Compensation
than $1 billion. We do not even know the exact amounts. Yet, the Hon. Member dares to say that we should not ask any questions about who these people are or how much they will receive. That is nothing more or less than a downgrading of the Parliament of Canada. It is an insult to this institution. Surely, the Hon. Member ought to recognize that.

Through you, Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell the Hon. Member what is insulting. It was insulting to work on the Finance Committee which for five or six months held hearings across the country-and I was in attendance at practically every one of those meetings-while some Hon. Members opposite seemed to spend more time with the television cameras in Vancouver and Calgary than they did at the meeting table. Having heard all the deliberations, we now come to decide what we do about the situation. Let us deal with the report-writing stage which started last week and which met for three full days. Members of the Hon. Member's Party were in attendance at the hearings over the number of months which they took place and yet his Party did not send one of its members to help in the preparation of the report. They did not even send a message to the Chairman to explain why they would not be able to attend that critical stage of the whole process. I admire the Hon. Member who can get to his feet with his histrionics and rhetorics waving his flag. However, I wish the members of his Party would have had a little more respect. The meeting with respect to the report writing was behind the scenes. It was an in camera meeting and television cameras were not in attendance. If members of his Party had attended, then they would have had to roll up their sleeves to do some work. If they would contribute in that way, then the Hon. Member might make a little more sense as well.
In closing, I stick to my comments. I think they are valid and right for Canadians. I think if we were to take a poll of Canadians we would find them telling us to stick with it because that is what they want.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate. The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp).

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate on the amendment that the House decline the giving of second reading to Bill C-79 to compensate the uninsured depositors in the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank.
The brief exchange during the last period of questions and comments has usefully disposed of the key points which the preceding speaker has made. What I would like to do in considering the question is return to some of the larger matters before us which the Government should have considered and which the Parliament of Canada has a real obligation to consider. Clearly, we have an important problem before us. We have a matter of bank failure. No one can doubt that. We have the fact of a ministerial failure, a failure by Government, which it would seem to me is equally apparent and which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) should long since have recognized in providing some type of an answer.
Late last winter we saw the difficulties with respect to the Canadian Commercial Bank and a rescue package was put forward. Gradually we had a revelation of what was wrong with the situation. Then, suddenly, just before this session of Parliament resumed, it was announced that not only had the Canadian Commercial Bank fallen but the Northland Bank had fallen as well. At an earlier stage we were told that the situation could be saved. The Government put together a rescue package. Then, we had the failure. Now, we have the suggestion being made that the cause of the failure was not necessarily the mismanagement of the bank. In fact, we have heard a good deal of partisan slanging in the House with respect to the preceding Government's policies being responsible for the difficulties which have arisen.
Whatever the source of the problem may have been, the reality is that the Government's supervision of the financial system of Canada has been inadequate, which has led to the taxpayers of Canada being faced with the need to pay hundreds of millions of dollars. In fact, when this Bill becomes an act, if it does, it will mean a cost of $875 million. It is possible that the cost of this liquidation will be a lot more than that. The Deposit Insurance Corporation, which is responsible for the insured depositors up to $60,000 under the existing law, is $1.2 billion in the red. If there is to be rapid repayment to the insured depositors of their $420 million, it is quite possible that the taxpayers will have to advance that money, if they don't end up to be actually responsible for it. They policy this Government is following will put us over the $1 billion mark in its attempt to clean up the mess which has developed in these two banks.
I would like to say something about how that situation developed. I am talking in terms of the economic difficulties of the early 1980s. The high interest rates forced on us by the Americans were just as hard on us as any policies followed by the Canadian Government. Those high interest rates slowed down economic activity in this country.
The failure of these banks is because of a long history of arbitrary power held by Canadian banks. They have refused to be subject to inspection by any public authority. In fact, there is a very long history of the banks of Canada saying "We will take care of ourselves. You stay out of it". One can go back to the time of the last bank failure in the early 1920s, and find, quite interestingly, that the bankers held to the position they had always held back to the beginning of the century and earlier, that they would take care of themselves, their investors, shareholders and depositors. The public authorities had to stay out of it. Back in those days, one banker, H. C. McLeod of the Bank of Nova Scotia, argued that there should in fact be inspection of the banks but he did not really get very far. The system of inspection which gradually evolved with the Inspector General of Banks is, I believe, recognized by all of us to be inadequate. Given such a situation, which I think the last Government knew about, and which is certainly no secret to the present Government, there should have been the most anxious care taken when it became clear that there were
October 9, 1985

difficulties in some of the banks. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) should have immediately looked at this situation when the present Government assumed power.
The arbitrary power of the banks, incidentally, Mr. Speaker, is very well exemplified in their opposition to organization by their workers. This is the situation in Toronto at the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce where its workers are attempting to achieve recognition and negotiate a first agreement. The attempts of the banks, not just in Toronto but across the country, to prevent the workers from exercising their right of association, which the Charter of Rights and Freedoms has attempted to establish for Canadians in all their varied circumstances, is a good illustration of how the banks today will still have it their own way and the devil take the hindmost. It does not seem to matter whether the issue involves overworked and underpaid workers, or the taxpayers of the country who must face the consequences of abusive power and irresponsible lending and the bank failures which result from that.
The matter of the irresponsibility of the Ministers involved is quite vital to the confidence of Canadians generally, and of the people in our financial institutions, in our Government. It seems to me that there is no choice but to say that the Department of Finance, whether under the Minister of Finance or under the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) acted irresponsibly in this situation. Whatever the causes of the difficulties may have been, the fact that a bail-out package was put together so quickly, and others were sucked into it, that guarantees were given and then the institutions were allowed to go on about their business for several months before it became clear what the situation was, allows one to conclude that the responsibility which the Minister of Finance should have exercised was entirely lacking.
It is laudable, after 62 years of no bank failure in this country, to be determined not to let the first one occur at this early point in a new Government's life. However, it is not laudable to think that the statements of the bank were accepted. If the Minister of Finance had known anything of Canadian banking history, he would have realized that these institutions got into difficulties sometimes because their officers and executive were irresponsible and loaned money on assets which were not sufficient and they were prepared to play fast and loose with the books. One would have thought that anyone with any measure of prudence when faced with this situation would have decided that a very close look should be taken. I am not particularly impressed when the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) argues that it takes a great deal of expertise to assess the quality of land, buildings or what have you, because it is not really the buildings or land which are the banks assets, it is the loans which have been incurred by others which are owed to the bank. It should not take a very long time to consider the payment record on those loans and determine whether in fact they are solid assets.
It seems to me that a relatively small group of people, given the free run of the bank, as they should have had that weekend, would have discovered pretty quickly that there were all kinds of supposed assets on which payment was not forth-
Depositors Compensation
coming, assets which would have to be drastically written down if not tossed out completely. It is precisely out the failure of the Department of Finance, and its officials, to ensure that that kind of review was taken that a profound difficulty arose. Instead, the Government put together a package and tried to assure Canadians that this institution was safe, and it is that action which Ministers and private Members support as responsible action. Once the Government had involved itself in that way, it would feel politically and, at the very least, morally responsible for the institution. The taxpayers of Canada face the abominable result. They face a situation in which the existence of a Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation is inadequate to solve the problem. They face a situation in which the Government thinks it has no choice but to turn to them to provide the funds to cover these enormous deposits which the insurance would not cover.
Therefore, it is in fact the failure of the Minister of Finance and of the Minister of State for Finance and their officials. They the Ministers, of course, are the persons responsible to this Parliament. It is their failure to ensure that what they were doing was properly done. It is their failure, once they had involved themselves, to ensure that what they were presuming to guarantee would in fact continue to stand which has created a situation in which $1 billion, give or take, and who knows how much more by the time the banks have been liquidated, is going to come out of the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada.
The Minister of Finance is preoccupied with deficit reduction. He is very concerned about reducing the call on the lenders of Canada. Yet he faces a situation in which his deficit is increased by $1 billion. What does that do to create confidence in this Government which presumed to be so businesslike? There have been appalling failures in regulation, in supervision and in the responsibilities of the Department of Finance. If we did not have such a shabby Government, Mr. Speaker, as it appears to be these days, with the departure of some Ministers while others-admittedly higher in the Cabinet pecking order-continue on, we would surely have had happen what, in the long traditions of Parliament, is the only honourable course. The Minister of Finance would have given up his position, would have said, "If I am compelled by the mistakes I made last winter to demand $1 billion from the Canadian taxpayers, I have to go". The Prime Minister would then have to find someone who could renew the confidence of the Canadian people in the Government, the House of Commons, these persons in the Canadian financial system and throughout our society. The Prime Minister should have long since asked for the Minister's resignation. He should have found himself a Minister of Finance who was not such a babe in the woods, who recognized the importance of his job and that it was just not a matter of trying to reduce the deficit he is responsible for, but that the institutions of the Government, and the financial and economic institutions of the country have to be maintained in their proper way.
When, because of the irresponsibility of this Government, the taxpayers face a Bill to totalling $1 billion, what are they

to do? It will be three years before the next election but I do not imagine they are going to forget these things. If the ladies and gentlemen to the number of 211 who came here thought they would reign on for some indefinite period, I suspect that the further back one goes the more doubt there must be about this piling up of mistakes and irresponsibility on the part of Ministers. One can only hope that because of the wisdom gained through contemplating the next election we will see some measure of responsibility.
This Bill does not deserve to be passed. The taxpayers of this country do not deserve to pay the Bill. If they have to pay it, they demand that responsibility be exercised by the Prime Minister. They demand that the Minister of Finance go and that we get someone we can really trust.
