Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to speak in the debate on Bill C-79. I was disappointed in the paucity of verisimilitude displayed by the previous speaker. I am also disappointed in a newspaper which used to portray itself as one of Canada's great newspapers, my own city's Edmonton Journal, which said in an editorial on October 2:
By trying to blame the Liberals for the collapse of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, the government shows it is bankrupt of any sense of responsibility for its actions.
We have an example here of responsibility to small depositors, credit unions, and charitable organizations across Canada. We have a demonstration of responsibility not only to western Canada but to all parts of this country. Come election time I think that responsibility and its exercise will be recognized in the most positive fashion.
We have as well a responsibility in some way to redress the wrongs whereby, due to the National Energy Program, $17 billion were sucked, sumped and siphoned out of the economy of western Canada. To compound that indignity by siphoning another $1 billion out of the western economy would be the most grievous fault, immoral, unethical and wrong politically. We could have slimed out of it, I suppose, but we face our responsibilities. We do not slime as others might have done.
Western banks will some day grow and thrive and we hope that time of healing will arrive soon. There are some nascent western banks now which we hope will weather this storm. We hope that a new atmosphere of trust can be built on the solid plan which is before us in Bill C-79. The consequences, had these banks gone under in March, would have been absolutely devastating to western Canada.
Why should we compensate the uninsured depositors? That is the first question that has to be answered. As the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) has said many times in
this House and outside, we are compensating these ordinary Canadians because the situation facing the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank reflects unique and particular circumstances. These two banks accounted for less than 1 per cent of the total assets of the Canadian banking system. However, they provided important support to economic activity in western Canada at a critical time.
A word now, Mr. Speaker, about the context in which these banks grew. The western economy grew rapidly because of the energy boom in the late 1970s. During that boom capital was short in Alberta, and the new banks recognized their opportunity to supply the demand. Because of the boom conditions the banks depended mainly on the energy, real estate and construction sectors which were growing most rapidly. That is the context in which the banks fell. No one in Alberta or in western Canada, or indeed anywhere in Canada except perhaps the cabal which perpetrated the NEP upon us, predicted the critical recession which hit in the early 1980s and came to its nadir in 1982. No one could predict the depth of that depression, for that is what it was in Alberta, from which the western economies have still not recovered. To a large extent that depression was imposed on the western economies by the national Government in the form of the NEP. This policy gravely destabilized the economic situation in western Canada and it came at the same time as major fluctuations in world energy market conditions and the U.S. deregulation of gas prices. Alberta and the other energy producing provinces experienced much uncertainty and loss of confidence in the oil and gas industry, and consequently in the real estate industry, especially regarding investment. These were, of course, the very sectors upon which the CCB and the Northland Bank depended.
I would like to make reference, if I may, to the remarks of the distinguished Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) made in this House on October 7. That gentleman said, and he was referring to September 1 and September 9 when Parliament reconvened:
We on this side of the House were conned that time. We were conned. The chartered banks were sucked in.
Earlier in the same speech he also said:
That bank was badly managed from its inception.
The question that remains is: If the bank was badly managed, where was the right hon. gentleman's Party for the first seven or eight years of its life? Where were they?
He was where he is right now, out of the House.

The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition said that the Official Opposition supported the emergency procedures, the bail-out if you like, because it was told the bank was experiencing a few temporary problems due to some questionable management decisions. The bail-out, Mr. Speaker, was designed to be successful and render the bank solvent and viable once again. That was the basis for our Government's decision at that time. The western Canadian economy was far less stable than was thought at that time. That is not the whole explanation for the collapse of these banks, but that
October 9, 1985

is for Mr. Justice Estey to decide. However, it must not be underestimated in any discussion of the banks' failure. The economy of Alberta in particular is still suffering the effects of the NEP. According to figures from the Conference Board and Statistics Canada, the unemployment rate in Alberta, which rose from 3.9 per cent in 1979 to 10.8 per cent in 1983, is down slightly this year but it still stood at 9.7 per cent last August. Housing starts numbered 39,947 in 1979 and fell to 17,000 in 1983, and the Conference Board forecast for 1985 is a mere 5,900. Clearly this sector has not recovered from the devastation of the NEP. Some further statistics. In the construction industry the value of work purchased in millions of dollars went from a peak of 14,491 in 1981 to 9,674 in 1984. The Conference Board forecast for this year is 10,835. The real estate industry is still in a serious slump. There are sales going on in the residential field but the prices are bottoming out. While the average value for a Multiple Listing System transaction reached $106,788 in 1981, in the second quarter of 1985 it was down to $79,053, the lowest in a decade.
What is the responsibility of the Government in this whole situation? It has to be to recognize that the blame for the collapse of these banks cannot be placed squarely on any one Party. Our bank regulatory system certainly needs improvement. I think the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) detailed that for us. The CCB's loan portfolio was in a more serious condition than was made apparent in March. The support package did not entirely succeed in restoring market confidence in the CCB and deposits eroded steadily. As the Minister of State for Finance said, those who kept their deposits in these western banks during the depression helped to cushion the serious impact of the recession on western Canadians. As the Minister of State has also said, unless those depositors are compensated quickly, their losses will result in job lay-offs.
The uninsured depositors of these banks include provincial Governments, municipalities, Government agencies, colleges, hospitals, individuals, small businesses, small financial institutions, Canadian and, yes indeed, foreign banks, investment dealers, and credit union centrals. The Government depended on the support of the depositors who continued to participate in the effort to preserve the viability of an important financial institution.
At stake is a larger element of credibility. The long-term larger issue has to do with our credibility world-wide. Much can be made of the inter-relationship of the banking system of Canada with that of the world. We have to recognize that the Government of Canada must send a strong signal to the rest of the world that banking in Canada is safe. This legislation does a great deal to drive that point home. I notice that the Federal Reserve Board of the United States has said that it will increase the frequency of bank examinations and make other changes to strengthen bank supervision. That is another country where these difficulties are being recognized and met head on.
Depositors Compensation
I would like to say a few words about the responsibility factor of the Government. The Member from Thunder Bay appears not to have confidence in the Cabinet Ministers responsible for this decision and this legislation. I would like to go on record saying that I have nothing but the highest admiration for the steadfastness, serenity, consistency and candour of the Minister of State for Finance and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) of this country. For that reason, I am speaking in support of this Bill as an Edmontonian, an Albertan, and a Canadian. It is time to stand in defence of our banking system, of regional banks, and of Bill C-79 which will restore confidence and bring justice and equity to the ordinary people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, as has been mentioned on several occasions in the House, it was only last March that the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) stood in her place and gave the House unequivocal assurances. She said in effect that if Parliament would approve an aid package, a bail-out for the Canadian Commercial Bank of $225 million, all Members of the House could be assured of several things. First, she said that they could be assured that the bank would then become viable. Second, she said that in short order the bank would become profitable and, third, that in due course the money that the Government had advanced would be returned to the Government so that the taxpayers would not be out of pocket in the long run. Finally, she said that by doing this we would ensure that other banks would be protected from failure.
These assurances were given and my Party accepted them in good faith. Among the reasons that we did so is that my Party believes in the decentralization of the banking system. We believe that well-managed, well-run, competently administered regional banks are good for Canada. There is no question that they are needed. However, the corollary is that badly run banks, trust companies, credit unions, or any other financial institutions deserve no support whatsoever and certainly deserve no special consideration from the Parliament of Canada.
Let us talk about good management. We now all have copies of the report by George C. Hitchman. On page 3 he said that he advised Mr. McLaughlan, President of the Canadian Commercial Bank, that moving a bad loan to a new name and showing it as a good loan was unacceptable. Well, Mr. Speaker, so much for well run or badly managed regional banks. The Minister of State for Finance gave the House assurances which were backed up by her senior colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), himself. Those Ministers have been proven wrong. Now that we are faced with Bill C-79, my Party says, "Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me". That is why we will not support Bill C-79.
The incompetence that has been demonstrated in this bank fiasco goes well beyond the two Ministers in question. It involves the entire Government and that is frightening. When the Minister of State for Finance was asked whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had interfered and caused her and the Minister of Finance to act against their better judgment

October 9, 1985
Depositors Compensation
she replied that it was a collective decision. That is an admission that in dealing with this matter and making a $1 billion blunder the entire Government of Canada revealed its lack of competence and that it does not possess good judgment. That is the issue with respect to Bill C-79. The Canadian people and Parliamentarians are not being fooled at all by hiding the truth behind some far-fetched and phoney reference to the National Energy Program or the lack of concern for regional financial institutions or the lack of caring about western Canada. We can all see through that guise.
This bank failure fiasco is the most distressing and most disturbing public issue perhaps in this century, certainly within the time of my generation. This fiasco is costing Canadian taxpayers $1 billion. It is a $1 billion error at a time when there is little money available for genuine needs in this country. There is no money for expanding regional development programs or for all the direct job creation that we ought to have. There is not enough money to help the farmers. Laid-off workers who have lost their jobs as a result of plant closures have to spend their precious severance pay before they can draw unemployment insurance benefits. There is not enough money for foreign aid. There is no money to help native communities by giving them such basic things as a good supply of drinking water or the means to deal with sewage treatment. There is not enough money for any of those genuine needs, yet Parliament is being asked to provide $1 billion for uninsured depositors. Most of that money will go to foreign banks, Canadian banks, corporations, and other wealthy individuals.
There is one simple principle that I subscribe to which is shared by members of my Party and that is that we should help first those who need it most. Bill C-79 is the reverse of that, it says to help first those who need it least. I know that some of my friends on the Government benches have already asked and would want to ask again what is to become of those charitable organizations, those poor municipalities, those small credit unions, and those pension funds. Let us clear up that issue. First of all, most of the payout will not go to those organizations at all. It will go to the foreign banks, Canadian banks, well-to-do corporations and wealthy depositors.
Second, we know that in cases of genuine need as a result of this or any other bank failure, the Government could be generous with the full support of Parliament and the bill would be much less than a billion dollars. Where hardship can be shown, help can be extend. There would be no problem because Canadians would expect no less of the Government and no less of Parliament.
However, I expect that in this list of depositors there would be very few who would fall into that category. Take, for example, the concern some Members have expressed for pension funds. Let us remember that nothing at all is being done for pension fund shareholders. They are at the end of the line and will, in all likelihood, get nothing.
Bill C-79 cannot be justified or rationalized on the basis of helping the poor, the needy or destitute. Bill C-79 is not a
"little guy's'' Bill. This bank fiasco issue can be understood in these terms: very big Government, the Government of Canada, new and inexperienced, became mixed up in the complexities of the financial world and got its fingers burned along with some of its well-to-do friends. Bill C-79 is not really a Bill to help anyone, it is a Bill to bail out the Government at taxpayers' expense. It is a Bill to save the Government from acute embarrassment caused by its inexperience and incompetence.
What we have seen in this bank fiasco issue is serious and grave mismanagement on the part of the Government of Canada. My constituents would be outraged with me if I were to vote in favour of Bill C-79.
While talking to my constituents in the last while, I have been saying that we must reduce our demands. We are living in a time of rising Government deficits and we must focus our attention on needs and may have to postpone our wants. Bill C-79 is not a needs Bill. It is a Government face-saving Bill.
Canadians are rapidly beginning to see that what is in charge and control here in Ottawa is incompetence. This bank failure fiasco will continue to haunt the Government until the dying days, just a few years hence. Parliament has been fooled. Its traditions have been trampled. There has been bad judgment and mismanagement. There has been a monumental bungling.
Now, the taxpayers of Canada are asked to dig down and fork out at least a billion dollars and perhaps more. Bill C-79 must be stopped dead in its tracks. That is my position and the position of my Party. When Canadians once again go into the polling booth, most of them will say that that was their position too.

Mr. Speaker, as a western member of the Finance Committee, I am glad to enter debate on Bill C-79 because I believe it is of particular importance to western Canada.
In March of this year, in good faith and based on available regulatory information, an attempt was made to preserve the viability of the Canadian Commercial Bank. That western regional-based financial institution, like all others in the western region, suffered considerable hardship as a result of global inflation and the disastrous effects of the National Energy Program. That program chased billions of dollars in investment out of Canada. It was a program of confiscation without compensation. It robbed Alberta of its vitality and caused serious ripple effects in the neighbouring provinces of British Columbia and my own Saskatchewan.
It should, therefore, be no great surprise that real estate values collapsed, along with other energy related assets in western Canada. The western based institutions, with a heavy loan concentration in energy and real estate, suffered a considerable erosion of their own security portfolios. In 1980, that security may have been fairly valued at 100 cents but today it is valued at perhaps 30 cents. The fate of those institutions that lent 50 cents or 60 cents on the dollar, on the face of that security, is quite evident.
October 9, 1985

The prime cause of failure of all of these western regional institutions, be they Canadian Commercial, Northland, Pioneer Trust, Western Capital Trust, Northwest or some of the credit unions, is quite clear. It was the tremendous loss of asset value owing to that infamous National Energy Program.
The Liberal Opposition whose policies caused these difficulties now seek, incredible as it may seem, to castigate the Government for an earnest attempt to preserve the integrity of the financial system and its western Canadian institutions. Had the Government allowed CCB to fail back in March, imagine the fuss, the hue and cry, the weeping and wailing and recrimination from the Opposition. The Government would have been categorized, quite properly, as being insensitive to western Canada. We would have displayed that same uncaring attitude to western Canada that characterized the previous administration.
The Opposition Parties, correctly I believe, agreed to the efforts to save CCB. Admittedly, with 20/20 hindsight, it now appears that attempt was doomed for two reasons about which neither the Government nor the Opposition was aware. The first was the run on deposits and the other was the eroded state of the loan portfolio. The key to this is the loan asset values-a faulty foundation which collapsed the financial house.
Why was more information not readily available? It now appears that the regulatory system was at fault. The rules for reporting, inspection, enforcement and supervision of the financial institutions are grossly deficient for today's marketplace. Some of these rules date back 60 or 70 years. They permit double counting of capital and the reporting of loan interest arrears in a way which make the loans appear current. They permit the taking of income on phoney restructuring deals, self-dealing and the milking of CDIC.
Most financial institutions are well run and well managed by competent and capable people. However, there are exceptions and today's rules require updating to deal with the unscrupulous. The financial community has shifted from the days of the clerk with the quill pen and green visor to the modern age of computers and electronic processing of information. It is an age in which even national boundaries mean little. We are now living in a global economy and the rules pertaining to the changing circumstances must be rewritten and codified.
It may be asked why this was not done earlier. I suggest that such a question be directed to the previous Government whose survivors now pretend to be in some state of anxiety over this Bill, one which enables payment to the depositors of these institutions who listened in good faith and lent their support to the rescue attempt. The Official Opposition, when in power for the previous 20 years, not only laid the seeds for destruction of these western institutions, not only destroyed Canadian unity, but also had the opportunity to write new rules and regulations for the conduct, management and governance of the institution. Did they do so? No. They failed in the area of financial regulation just as they failed in the energy sector and in every other way. They left our Government with a mess of monumental proportions and now stand in the House, apparently
Depositors Compensation
without shame, seeking to shift the blame for their mismanagement and inadequacies, their lack of concern and squalid performance.
They seek to load all this baggage on a new Government which noted the need to reform the regulations of the institutions from the day it took office. Our Government announced its intention to do so last November. During the winter, the Government developed a discussion paper-the Green Paper on the Regulation of Institutions which was issued in the spring. This Green Paper has been studied almost daily by the Finance Committee. Extensive hearings have been held and its report is now being formulated. That report will lead to new legislation that will update and modernize regulations and provide means for inspection, supervision and enforcement. It will provide for sanctions and penalties for self-dealing and conflicts. That report will deal with deposit insurance and hopefully signal a new era in federal financial regulations so that all Canadians will know the rules and limits and adhere to them.
Clearly, the Government has paid more attention to the financial institutions in the past 12 months than the previous Government did in 20 years. The Government is committed to national reconciliation and economic renewal. The rescue attempt was part of that process. So too is this Bill which should now be read a second time and sent to committee.
Some of the questions being raised by Members do not appear to be related to the principle of the Bill. I believe that the committee is the appropriate place to deal with some of those questions. We must remember that it is the principle of Bill C-79 that ought to concern us today.
The Bill is intended to do something that is not without precedent in our system. Just last spring we were dealing with another Bill which did very much the same thing for depositors in Pioneer Trust. At that time I do not recall any prolonged call for the names of the individual depositors who were to receive reimbursement for the uninsured portions of their deposits. When we look at the contents of this Bill we must be struck by the element of simple justice that it contains. It offers an unusual but appropriate solution for the problems faced by many people in western Canada.
I know that some members of the Official Opposition may find it difficult to relate to the problems of western Canada but this Government considers it a priority and a duty to respond to legitimate calls made on it from all parts of the country.
What is the solution? Clearly the solution is to move to reimburse the uninsured depositors.
No, it is not.

The Minister of State made the very point on Monday, when she spoke to this Bill, that its provisions were not to be taken as precedents. The provisions are unusual but they are also appropriate to a

October 9, 1985
Depositors Compensation
particular situation, and they meet reasonable expectations of those most intimately involved with the present problem, the depositors.
Although this point of view has been dismissed by the Opposition I think it is important as we look at this matter to remember why many of the individuals and small businesses are involved at all in the affairs of CCB. After the events of last March it would be unreasonable to have expected individual depositors to conclude that the bank was unsound and to have removed their deposits. Indeed, fairly clearly the federal Government, the chartered banks and the two provinces which participated in the rescue package did not want depositors to withdraw.
It may well be that if there were a way to differentiate between depositors as to those who were sophisticated enough to take a chance, knowing their options, that they could be excluded from the Bill. However, there would still remain those who trusted the words and actions of two levels of Government and the chartered banks. Such depositors, by and large, are those who do not have the facilities to make complicated judgments about banks. They are people who have savings, perhaps after a lifetime of hard work, which they left in the CCB on the apparent recommendation of the Government.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, it appears that some Hon. Members are suggesting that there is no urgency about helping these people out of a problem which they did not create themselves.
As for the option of reimbursing some depositors, but not all, I find it hard to believe that this could be seriously entertained by anyone. It could not be done by class of depositor without singling out one or two groups of institutions for discriminatory treatment. Would we send the message that foreign banks could not expect equal treatment? Would we tell labour unions or pension plans that they are not to expect the same treament that we propose for individuals and small businesses?
I see no advantage to anyone in keeping this Bill from committee. There is urgency in the matter, and I ask all Hon. Members to agree to give this Bill second reading, and let the committee start its work. Thank you.

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by saying that I am sick up to here listening to the Conservatives try to tell the public that somehow or other the legitimate objections that have been raised to this Bill have something to do with an anti-western feeling.
Right on.
I am fed up with it. It is wrong, and to continue to say it is an abomination on Parliament.
You are certainly not going to get any western sympathy.
Let me put it quite bluntly-
You do it every day.

This attempt by this ragtag group sitting over here to try to convince Canadians that somehow or other because we are concerned about the Government of Canada spending, inappropriately I might say, something in the order of $3 billion is somehow to be considered as anti-western Canada is a shame on the Conservative Party and not on the rest of the Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: What about the depositors?

Let me deal with the problem as I see it. This is not an east versus west problem. This is a large bank versus small bank problem. There is not a small bank in this country that is not now suffering because of the economic policies pursued by the right wing Liberal and now Conservative Governments that have ruled this country since its inception.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext: You ought to know, you put them in.

Let me tell you about this. Do you know why this bank is in trouble? Large banks, the big ones, the Royal, the Bank of Montreal, the Imperial Bank of Commerce and the others can afford to loan money at lower interest rates. Why? They can afford to do it because they are able to cream off the best possible customers. They get the first crack at the best customers. Small banks on the other hand, in order to lure depositors, offer higher interest rates on deposit. Nobody disagrees with that, I hope. However, in giving higher interest rates for deposits they must charge higher rates for loans. The best customers are not prepared to pay the higher interest rate for loans so the small banks therefore have to settle for less than the most affluent, less than the best, risks.
What they end up doing, and these banks are good examples, and there are others, is loaning money to people who are a higher risk. The end result of that is that they have a much higher risk portfolio, and the chance therefore of failure when you carry the highest of the high risk portfolios is clearly more evident. That is the problem in the banking system, that the big banks get the best and the smaller institutions have to take what is inevitably a much higher risk portfolio. It has nothing to do with east and west. It happens all across the country. So for God's sake start dealing with the reality. I am offended when this kind of ridiculous argument is proffered by certain people that somehow or other because you do not happen to live in Calgary that you do not understand the problems of a Calgary businessman, or you do not understand the problems of a Calgary home owner, or you do not know what it is like to be unemployed in Calgary.
You don't understand it.
Damn it all, it is no different being unemployed in Calgary, my friend-
You are full of nonsense.

-than it is to be unemployed in St. John's, than it is to be unemployed in Halifax, than it is to be unemployed in Hamilton. If you cannot find a job it makes no difference where you live.
October 9, 1985
You don't know anything about Alberta.
And that is the trouble with these people.

You know nothing about Alberta and
spare us the pomposity.
Let me go back a bit to the early part of the 1980s, for the benefit of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) who likes to shout but does not like to listen.
I don't have to listen to your nonsense.
Back in the 1980s when interest rates were up in the high teens and reaching into the low twenties, back in the 1980s when we were saying to the then Government-
Sanctimonious pomposity.

-that a serious economic problem was being brought about in a variety of different sectors of the economy and that unless the Government moved in to protect those sectors by bringing interest rates down there were going to be bankruptcies in almost every single area, the Conservatives together with the Liberals said nothing could be done about it.
We argued that there had to be measures taken to bring the interest rates down in order that home owners who were on the verge of losing their homes because they could not afford to pay the 20 per cent and 21 percent being asked by the banks. When we said that the Government should move to protect those individuals from losing everything they had worked for, the Tories joined with the Liberals and said nothing could be done about it.
When we said that small business people in every community, including in western Canada, were facing difficulty as a result of very high interest rates, that they could not afford to carry the merchandise and when they could afford to carry the merchandise they could not find markets because there was unemployment in much larger numbers than they could anticipate, and we said to them that the banks were taking unfair advantage of those people by charging them in the high teens and low twenties for the necessary moneys to carry on their businesses, and forcing them into bankruptcy, we said to the Conservatives, join with us in a battle to bring down interest rates. They said nothing could be done.
When the farmers were outside here complaining about the fact that they could not keep their family farms because the interest rates were so high that they could not meet their commitments, they could not even pay their feed costs; they could not pay their seed costs; could not pay the costs of running the farms, and when we said to the Government of the day back in 1982 and 1983 that we needed to bring down interest rates in order to save those individuals, the Conservatives joined with the Liberals and said nothing could be done about it.
If nothing could be done for the people losing their homes, their businesses and their farms, if nothing could be done for

the 1.5 million unemployed people who were losing everything for which they had ever worked, why is it that, because of a few friends who happen to be in the banking industry, the Conservative Party, now that it is the Government of Canada, can find $3 billion to bail them out?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Why is the steam coming out?

I will tell the Hon. Minister why the steam is coming out. I am sick and tired of listening to the garbage which is being spewed across the floor of the House by certain Hon. Members who do not know what happened in the period leading up to this Parliament. The problem with which we are now dealing stems from the time when the Conservative Party, in Opposition, refused to join with us in a battle against high interest rates. I remember the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), as the then opposition finance critic, standing at a podium in Montreal when high interest rates were the issue of the day and saying that if they were the Government, they would not do anything much different, that what the Liberals were doing was really all that could be done. After driving people out of their homes, off their farms and out of business, after failing to recognize what it was like when unemployment insurance ran out and there was not a penny available, there is no way to convince me that I should acquiesce and rush this Bill through to committee or that I should hurry it through so that this money can be paid. Small depositors are covered to $60,000 immediately. I say to the Conservatives that those depositors who need it will get their $60,000.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: How about the municipalities?
The municipalities are well covered by the provinces, at least those in the Province of Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: What about British Columbia?
I cannot answer for the Social Credit Government of British Columbia. I mean, it is anachronism.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: What about Manitoba?

Let us deal with reality. The fact of the matter is that we are being asked to say to those people for whom nothing could be done when the banks were ripping them off right, left and centre, that they should dig into their pockets after having lost everything they own and pay higher taxes to give the banks their money. I want to say, with only one minute remaining, no way. Those same banks sat and looked into the eyes of people who were crying because they were losing everything. Those same banks said to them: "We cannot help you because the banking practice demands that we have adequate collateral for a loan. Since you do not have it, you will have to lose your farm; we will sell off everything you own". When those same banks are crying at my doorstep and asking me to help them, I say to hell with them.

Mr. Speaker, I am now being provided with an opportunity to speak on Bill C-79 and the amendment thereto. The Government is

October 9, 1985
Depositors Compensation
asking us to appropriate $875 million, to be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund. In more simple terms, it is asking us to pay $875 million out of the pockets of taxpayers. I am speaking in support of the amendment of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), which makes clear that we on this side of the House in the Official Opposition wish to decline to give second reading to a Bill that in effect does not give us any idea as to whom these funds are being given. We have been denied the right to know the identity of the recipients of this money.
Traditionally, at least in the British tradition, in the Mother of Parliaments, for century upon century, the House of Commons has been responsible for the raising and spending of funds. It is our right and our privilege to say that and to do that as the Parliament. In the Parliament of Canada it is the duty of everyone of us, whether on the Government benches or on this side of the House, to demand to know where the taxpayers' money is going. Every Member of the House should not allow a Bill to be passed which in effect writes out a blank cheque. This is a general observation but if for no other reason than principle alone, we have reason to say that we will not pass this Bill. We also have further reasons to be doubtful about the wisdom of passing it.
We remember with great anguish and disappointment last March that when the Canadian Commercial Bank was experiencing difficulties, the Government came to Parliament and proposed that Parliament participate in a $255 millon bail-out. We were urged to participate in it. We were assured by the Government that it had to be done quickly, that time was a factor, and that we had to pass it so that others would not suffer. Having listened to the promises made, we were also assured by this Government which claims competence that the $255 million bail-out would in fact set the situation straight or set the bank up in a sound or solid condition, and that from then on we could look to a good future. That was back in March when we were told that all would be well. However, what we did not know and what the Government did not tell us was that many people in the Department of Finance had grave doubts about the package and about whether they had enough information to make an assessment or to recommend to the Parliament of Canada that it should participate in a $255 million bail-out package. The more we read, the more we learn and as more layers of the onion are peeled, we discover that the Government knew very little about the situation at that time. As time went on it began to discover that perhaps 30 cents on the dollar was the worth of the bank and that things were not well. Many of the players involved were wondering about whether they had enough information. The Government of Canada did not tell us the truth. It did not tell us what these other people were saying. It did not breathe a word of doubt, but it assured us that all would be well. It was bad judgment, which means that billions of dollars will be ultimately spent by the Government to buy its way out of its mistakes. Of course it is now saying to us that we should look after the depositors in these banks, that we should put up this $875 million to pay 100 cents on the dollar back to the depositors.
We are not talking in every case about depositors who have their life savings in these banks. Those with their life savings are at least protected up to $60,000. For example, if such a person has $60,000 in some kind of deposit account and another $60,000 in an RRSP, he or she might be protected up to the $120,000. No, it is not the little person who is being hurt. In fact, it is those who gambled their money in order to obtain high interest rates. We are being asked to protect depositors but, interestingly enough, the Government has not asked us to think about the shareholders. Why, I have to ask myself, in the name of morality, common sense and decency, is the Government making two categories of people? One category is the depositors who are protected up to $60,000 and the other is the shareholders who are not protected. It could be that some people became shareholders in these banks and put up their life savings thinking that such banks were good investments. The Government has once again failed to show intelligence and common sense. There is a double standard here. The depositors are treated one way and the sharehoolders another.
We are being asked to put up this money. The Government is not giving any money to the shareholders but it wants to give money to all the depositors. We want to see a list of these depositors. The Government wants us to take the taxpayers' money and pay it out to a list of faceless people and faceless international banks, corporations and speculators. It wants us to pay them with the taxpayers' money and it will not even tell us their names.
Those who simply want to collect their $60,000 need not tell us their names. However, why should we be paying in some cases over $1 million to an individual without knowing who that individual is? Why should we be paying millions of dollars to faceless organizations about which we know nothing? Members of Parliament are to write out a blank cheque made out to "To Whom It May Concern". I suggest that we have a bigger responsibility than that and we have a right, as the Leader of the Opposition has said, to demand of the Government a list of the names of these depositors.
Indeed, after looking back over what has happened and seeing the circumstances under which we were initially sucked into this bail-out scheme, I have to say that once bitten, twice shy. The Government assured us that everything was all right but we saw that things did not go as well as it promised. We saw that the Government did not take the time to allow bank executives, experts and auditors to look over the situation facing the Canadian Commercial Bank but told us that everything was fine. We certainly do not believe any longer that the Government has the trust and confidence that is required in order for us to vote for an $885 million blank cheque payable to unknown depositors.
When asking why the Government did this, I am afraid that we would have to come to some negative conclusions. We would have to come to the conclusion that the Government asked us to become involved in this scheme for political

reasons or perhaps to help out its friends but not because it knew the facts.
There has been much said about the deficit. Through the last Budget, we were told that the Government had to make certain cuts including billions of dollars worth of cuts in the education of young people. In fact, cuts to the old age pensions were proposed as were cuts to the family allowances, yet the Government can apparently afford to spend billions of dollars to bail out faceless depositors in a bank. The rich get richer. Their money is protected. The poor get poorer. They can lose their money and they can be reduced to further poverty. That is acceptable to the Government.
I do not see the deficit being refuced. I see the deficit rising because of the incompetence of the Government and its inability to deal properly with the problem of the Canadian Commercial Bank. I appeal to members of the Conservative Party to give to every Member of the House a list of the depositors so that we will not be asked to write out a blank cheque, something which is contrary to all traditions.

Mr. Speaker, it is for a tragic instance of the irresponsibility of this Government that we have to debate this Bill today. When I was elected, I little thought that we would see so quickly and completely a retreat from Tory principles as enunciated during the election campaign, but this is exemplified by the Bill before us today.
It does not surprise me that there are few members of the Government present in the House. Who would want to hear of the terrible record of the Government? It does not surprise me that they are sitting far apart and not speaking to one another. If they were speaking to one another, it could only be in terms of the abnegation of everything for which they campaigned as represented by this Bill.
I believe that the $875 million for which we are being asked to bail out the two failed banks is simply a down payment. We have it on the Minister's authority that this does not represent the final bill. Not only that but we have heard one of the most incredible statements I have ever heard a Minister make in this or any other democratically elected assembly. The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) has said:
-I want to make it perfectly clear that it is not the Government's intention to set a precedent in compensating uninsured depositors in our financial institutions.
With all due respect, Mr. Speaker, that is horse feathers and absolute nonsense. Every bankruptcy is a tragedy for the people involved. Every bankruptcy involves unique circumstances and unique situations. For the Minister to suggest that she is not setting a precedent is, with all due respect, unbelievable and 1 cannot believe that she does not recognize that that statement cannot be true.
The fact is that through this bail-out we are being called upon to authorize today, the Government is setting a precedent and avery dangerous one. Forgotten is the election rhetoric about freeing the free enterprise system and about opening Canada up for job creation. We are now looking at a bail-out of such gigantic proportions and such cataclysmic effects on

the budgetary accounts of the country that it is almost worthy of a Liberal Government rather than a Progressive Conservative Government.
The sort of bail-out at which we are looking is unprecedented both in its amount and in its purpose. As well, it is unpredecented in the circumstances that led to the Government considering its necessity. It would appear from the legislation that has been tabled in the House that the Government has been hijacked. It would appear that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his ever-diminishing ruling circle are merely Liberals who got into the Conservative Party just like the worm got into the apple and ate it out from the inside. They are saying to themselves, "Look what the other guys did for their corporate cronies. We had better show them that we can do just as well by our friends as the previous Government did by its friends". That would appear to me to be the entire motivation behind this Bill.
Much has been said from the Government benches. I am glad to see that Government members have enough self-respect to have now fallen silent. Much has been said about this Bill being for the protection of ordinary Canadians. I have not heard one argument that could sustain such an impertinent, nonsensical statement as that. Let us face the facts. We are not looking at mass unemployment as we might be if we were dealing with a manufacturing concern going bankrupt. We are looking at losses distributed right through the economy affecting people who ought to have known enough to verify the integrity, stability and strength of a financial institution before they put a penny into it, let alone the sort of sums that have been mentioned.
We are indeed being asked to sign a blank cheque because we are being asked to bail out a whole range of depositors who should have known better. These depositors include sophisticated investors, foreign banks, municipalities, provincial Governments, credit unions and smaller investors, the largest number of which should have and I believe did have access to the sort of information that would have warned them. For example, the City of Hull, whose manager spoke on the radio yesterday, sounded the warning which should have gone off in a lot of brains in Canada's financial community.
Notwithstanding the fact that the $60,000 will be paid to all depositors, with respect to insured portions, we are prepared to look at funding for those depositors who will undergo real hardship if this bail-out does not take place. However, a blank cheque in addition to the deficit of Canada or an increase in taxes for the people of Canada to pay for this bail-out-no, never, that is something that the Progressive Conservative Government should blush at introducing in the House, given the election rhetoric with which we were inundated during the last election campaign. I think it is worth repeating that the $60,000 sum is the statutory limit. If the Government goes ahead with its plan to pay depositors for investments above the $60,000-limit, where will the insurance industry in Canada be? What is the point in insuring against any form of risk?

We are not talking about widows' savings in this instance, nor are we talking about persons being reduced to ruin. We are not talking about the type of misery which a great financial loss can impose upon a single individual because, with good sense, we have the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation insuring deposits of individuals up to $60,000. Frankly, if it were not for the obvious lack of attention which the Government paid to this dossier over the summer, we would not now be facing the consequences of the improperly structured bail-out package which was put together last March.
Much has been made by the Government of the fact that these are both western financial institutions which were, indeed, adversely affected by the collapse of the western economy brought on by certain aspects of the National Energy Program introduced by the previous administration. I think that is something which is worthy of consideration and examination. We should say that apart from the unfortunates who are employees of the said banks, the losses, will be spread across Canada-rather, not the losses but the costs the Government will impose upon the country by this breath-takingly irresponsible piece of legislation. We have not heard one single spokesperson from the Government side speak about whether the $1 billion, or whatever it adds up to, is to be raised by taxation or whether it is to be raised by further borrowing. That is a clear dereliction of the Government's duty, along with its concealing of the list of depositors. They are also concealing from the people on which side of the ledger the bill will come down. Is it to be by a further augmentation of the deficit? One of the main planks in the Conservative campaign platform was that it would not raise the deficit. Will the Government increases taxes on the people of Canada when every inclination it has shown thus far is that it will try to hold the line with respect to taxation by cutting benefits to the elderly and the poor while paying off some of its supporters through numerous and sundry tax breaks and incentives such as the $500,000 capital gains exemption?
Mr. Speaker, my time is up, which is just as well because my breath is almost exhausted from the indignation and outrage which I feel at this most irresponsible action by the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I was going to say that I am pleased to rise in my place today. However, if I said that I would be misleading the House right off the bat. I am not pleased. I am irate. I am upset. I am disappointed. I wish to get a few things off my chest.
I wish to remind the House that we speak today on the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) to Bill C-79 which the Government has put forward to bail out its corporate buddies. The amendment indicates that the House declines to give second reading to a Bill, the principle of which is to permit payments of large, but unspecified amounts of public moneys-not the Government's money, not my money, not the money of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) or the money of the Cabinet but the taxpayers' money. We decline to pay out in a blind, deaf and dumb fashion without any knowledge of where the dollars are going and to whom they are going. The process of doing that in a blind, deaf and dumb manner reduces not only the right of Parliament-I don't give a damn about Parliament's right-but the responsibility of Parliament to be accountable for taxpayers' dollars. That is the first responsibility of any Opposition in a parliamentary system. It is an adversary system. They separate us by two sword lengths to keep us apart because it gets heated at times. However, we are not here because we want to spend our days nit-picking over departmental expenditures. It is our responsibility to be the public watchdog of the taxpayers' purse. We are being asked to spend handsome sums from that purse with no accountability whatsoever as to where and how that money is to be spent.
I have been in my riding in recent days. I have had an opportunity during those days to spend some time talking to people who understand the notion of taking a risk. These people understand the concept of having the right to succeed. They also understand the concept of having the right to fail and expecting no one to pick them up. I met a small contractor in the Bay of Islands in the great riding of Humber-Port-au-Port-St. Barbe who spent 15 years putting together a family business. He performed various work around the west coast of Newfoundland. In the middle of a contract he had a bank step in and call a demand loan. When the bank called the loan he saw 15 years of sweat, hard work, hope and aspiration crumble before his very eyes.
I had a chance to talk to a fisherman on the great northern peninsula. This man has been fishing for 30 years. This year the fish just did not come to the great northern peninsula. We do not know why but it was a miserable season. That fisherman got four or five weeks of fishing in this year. He knows that in two weeks he will have to make his annual boat payment. He cannot make it because he has had a miserable year. They are going to call his loan, grab his boat, and he will not be a fisherman anymore. He is sad and disappointed and his aspirations have been crushed.

I talked to a small businessman in the town of Deer Lake who, together with his wife, mortgaged his house and went into the furniture business. They did a subcontract job for a large contractor. They spent several hundreds of thousands of dollars installing kitchen cabinets in an apartment building. But they did not get paid for the subcontract because the major contractor, who had the job, was in financial trouble. It ends up that the fellow who made no mistakes, who had done nothing wrong, is going to go under because the bank is calling his loan. And he is sad, disappointed and his dreams have been crushed.
Not one of these people, be it the fisherman, the small contractor or the furniture maker, who have had their lifesav-ings taken away from them have asked the Government of Canada to bail them out; nor has the Government of Canada offered to bail out these three people. We live in a system where we all have the right to take risks. We all have the right, or at least the opportunity, to succeed beyond our wildest dreams, but if we fall on our face and go broke, if we make a mistake, we must face the consequences.
It is more than I can swallow to know that honest, hardworking Canadians who have invested their time and capital and a good part of their lives in ventures and who, for whatever reason, have failed, have failed in silence, and no one has offered to bail them out, yet when a bank which is involved in bad lending practices, which is riddled with poor management, fails, we find that deposits of over $60,000 are going to be bailed out by the Government of Canada. The Government is going to step in and give them all this money, 60 per cent of which will not even stay in western Canada. I am tired of hearing this line that the bail-out is an attempt to help western Canada. Sixty per cent of the funds will not even stay in western Canada. It is a bail-out of large corporations. These people want the right to make $1 million but do not want the right to fail. They want the Governement to provide a cushion for them.
Every Prime Minister has to wear two hats. The first hat is a political hat. He puts that hat on when he is involved in an election campaign and goes out to stir up the troops, to inspire the team, to address the people, to sell his message, to garner support. That is his political hat. The other hat the Prime Minister must wear is that of chief executive officer. He is the man who is in charge, who is minding the store and looking after the taxpayers' purse. He is the man who makes the intelligent, rational, responsible and defensible decisions. This Government has a Prime Minister who has only one hat. It is his political hat. He has lost the hat of chief executive officer. He does not know where it is and neither do his Ministers.
A political decision was made by the Prime Minister last spring in the middle of an economic summit. He would not allow a bank to fail and ruin his television image. We could not have the veneer which was being developed scratched. We could not have a blip on an otherwise well managed media campaign. As a result, the people of Canada are being asked to

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join in this debate which deals with fairness, with how we treat banking institutions in this country and how clearly under this Government there are two classes; there are those which Government will help and there are those which it will not.

We are told that we do not have the money to continue to ensure that family allowances are fully indexed to the cost of inflation. As a result, we are now seeing the development of some difficulties. However, we do have enough money to bail out two banks. Whether it is $1 billion, $2 billion or $3 billion, only time will tell. But the reality is that it will cost the taxpayers of this country a large amount of their hard-earned dollars-their tax dollars-to pay for this decision of the Government of Canada.

For him it is a matter of principle as well as the money, and he is frustrated and angry that the Government is bailing out these two financial institutions but not the one he was involved in. He does not believe it is fair, and neither do I.
As I looked at this situation I asked myself what else this money could be used for. My riding and that of the adjoining riding, Thunder Bay-Nipigon, comprise about 113,000 people. If we spread that $1 billion among those people it would be a very nice little Christmas present, $9,000 per individual. We could say the same for any community in Canada. They would have more money to spend on consumer goods and they would pay more taxes. There are many innovative ways we could use that money. The way this Government has established its priorities in the bailing out of these two banks is inappropriate, and that is why I would be more than happy to join my colleagues in voting against this Bill, and to continue speaking against it through all stages.
The question has been raised concerning municipalities and the provinces and the money they had on deposit in these banks. While I appreciate the situation they may be in, I think it is a warning to municipalities and provinces to be careful about what they do with their taxpayers' money. They should not put it into risky situations. Rather, they should ensure that the money is in an institution which will not only continue to pay interest but continue to be viable. Therefore, I suggest to the Government that it would be wise to reconsider this attempt regardless of whether or not we get the names of the people involved. I do not believe in principle that we should be supporting this bail-out.
